speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESIGNATIONS AND APPOINTMENTS-ADDITIONAL PARLIAMENTARY ASSISTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce certain ministerial changes, and the appointment of additional parliamentary assistants.
I regret exceedingly to have to inform the house that, due to protracted illness, the Honourable J. Allison Glen has felt it necessary to tender his resignation as Minister of Mines and Resources, and that in existing circumstances I have felt it my duty to submit Mr. Glen's resignation to His Excellency the Governor General, and to advise its acceptance.
I cannot say how deeply I regret the severance of official relations with so highly valued a colleague in the government, and so old and loyal a friend. What I would most wish to say at this time is set forth in the correspondence which has passed between Mr. Glen and mj'self. It would, I believe, best explain the situation were I to read the correspondence to the house.
The day before yesterday I received by Canadian National Telegraphs the following telegram, dated at Winnipeg, Manitoba, June 9, 1948, at 8.27 p.m.:
The Right Honourable William Lyon Mackenzie King,
Prime Minister of 'Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
I have been informed today by my medical adviser that my illness may be protracted for an indeterminate period. I feel therefore that matters of urgent importance in my department requiring early consideration and decision may suffer by my continued absence, and I have consequently decided to submit my resignation as minister, to be acted upon in your discretion, which I herewith do.
May I add that it is with the deepest regret that I feel constrained to take this course, which severs the very happy ministerial association which it has been my privilege to enjoy with you and my colleagues in the cabinet, an association which I shall always gratefully cherish.
J. Allison Glen.
To that telegram I replied yesterday, June 10, 1948, as follows:
The Honourable James Allison Glen, M.P.,
541 Cambridge Street,
Winnipeg, Manitoba.
My dear Glen:
I have just received your telegram of yesterday. I am indeed deeply sorry lto learn that your strength has not returned as rapidly as we all hoped it might. If, as you say, there is a possibility of your illness being protracted, I think you are right in seeking to relieve yourself of the responsibilities of administering the affairs of the Department of Mines and Resources and giving yourself as much in the way of rest and freedom as possible. This should greatly assist you in expediting your recovery. In the circumstances, I have decided to submit your resignation to His Excellency forthwith and to advise its acceptance.
I need not assure you that it is with a regret equal to your own that, for the reasons mentioned in your telegTam, I feel it my duty to recommend the acceptance of your resignation. Before, however, making any recommendation to His Excellency, I should like to thank you warmly for the splendid service you have Tendered Canada as a minister of the crown, and for all that your helpful counsel and close cooperation has meant to our colleagues, and to myself in particular, in the work of the administration.
My deep regret at the severance of these happy and helpful relations will be shared, I know, in full measure by all our colleagues. Fortunately, your retirement from the ministry will not mean the loss of the association which, as members of parliament, we have enjoyed over so many years, and to the continuance of which, through the opportunity afforded you of rest and freedom from ministerial responsibilities, will, I trust, be assured for some time still to come.
With warmest personal regards to Mrs. Glen and yourself,
Believe me, as always, dear Glen,
Yours very sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King
I am sure hon. members generally will deeply regret, with my colleagues and myself, the Honourable Mr. Glen's retirement from the ministry, and especially the reason for it; we will all wish in deepest sincerity that his health may speedily be restored, and that we may see him again in parliament at the beginning of another session.
I wish now to announce the resignation of the Honourable James A. MacKinnon as Minister of Fisheries, and Mr. MacKinnon's
Changes in the Ministry

appointment as Minister of Mines and Resources, the department over which Mr. Glen presided and of which Mr. MacKinnon, during a portion of Mr. Glen's absence, has been the acting minister.
I have great pleasure also in announcing the appointment of Mr. Robert W. Mayhew as a member of the Privy Council of Canada, and as Minister of Fisheries. Mr. Mayhew will be British Columbia's representative in the cabinet.
I wish to announce the transfer of Mr. Robert H. Winters of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, from the position of Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue to that of Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport.
I announce further the transfer of Mr. Thomas Reid of New Westminster, British Columbia from the office of Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries to that of Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue.
It will be recognized at once that it would not be advisable that the parliamentary assistant in the Department of Fisheries should be from the same province as the minister of that department. The transfer of Mr. Reid from the Department of Fisheries to the Department of National Revenue will fortunately leave an opening for the appointment of a parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Fisheries from another province which, up to the present time, has not had representation in the house by way of a parliamentary assistant.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, may I say that in a return tabled on February 23, 1948, in answer to a question of mine, information regarding the payment of moneys under the war emergency training program was given in full by the Department of Labour. In a return, sessional paper 186B, May 17, similar full replies were given by the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Fisheries. But a letter contained in the return from the deputy minister of trade and commerce withholds the same type of information on the ground that "it is not considered to be in the public interest to give information as to subsidies paid to individual concerns."
Evident]}', in view of the other information in this return and the return of February 23, this statement of the deputy minister is not correct, and in my opinion is an interference with the privileges and rights of the members of parliament, who should be able to secure details of the expenditure of public moneys appropriated by or under the control of parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Public Works. I am well aware of the rule of the house that questions have to be brief and to the point, but in this particular instance my question is in connection with a disaster which has just occurred in my constituency, and I beg the indulgence of the house.
I have just returned from an inspection tour of the flooded areas of Bonaventure county, where I have conferred with several local delegations. The population of Bonaventure county living in the valleys of Nouvelle West river, Cascapedia river and Bonaventure river, as well as other districts, have been severely flood-stricken and have suffered loss and damages to the extent of over one million dollars.
For one full week, all communication by train and by highway was cut off between Bonaventure county, on the south shore of the Gaspe coast, and the rest of the province, on account of railway and highway bridges having been washed out.
At Nouvelle West there is a large area of cultivated land still lying under water, owing
to the fact that the Nouvelle river went out of its original channel to form three new channels to the sea.

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RELIEF FOR BONAVENTURE COUNTY

speechtext: Order. May I remind hon. members that I have been very generous in the last two weeks to hon. members who have asked questions concerning flood conditions in their constituencies. Hon. members should be fair to the hon. member who is asking the question.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RELIEF FOR BONAVENTURE COUNTY
speechtext: Alongside the Cascapedia river, in the Barry Mountain district, a road which is essential to lumber operations has been washed out for a distance of about thirty miles. It is estimated that 50,000 cords of pulpwood have been driven to the sea by the flood. My question is: what would the Minister of Public Works be prepared to do in order to help and relieve the flood-stricken population of Bonaventure county?

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RELIEF FOR BONAVENTURE COUNTY
speechtext: I believe I shall have to give the hon. member the answer I have given to other hon. members who brought their cases to my attention. Flood conditions generally do not come under the control of the federal government. We may take up the instance of a national disaster such as has occurred in British Columbia, but not ordinary flood conditions. Where navigation is unimpeded, we have no jurisdiction. That comes under provincial jurisdiction. If I understood the hon. member correctly, he said that a road has been covered by water. Roads come under the provincial government. I believe the provincial government has the responsibility of maintaining the roads or protecting them from damage.

I shall be pleased to abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I hope to discuss the matter on a later occasion, but I would ask the minister to be good enough, in connection with all agreements into which Canada enters, to give consideration to the shipment of goods through Canadian ports. That should be definitely written' into every agreement made by the Department of Trade and Commerce; otherwise I do not know how we shall get the business that rightly belongs to us. If someone is selling or buying goods, it is his privilege to indicate to the buyer or the seller, as the case may be, whether 'he wishes the goods shipped by freight, express, water, or rail, and whether they should be Shipped via Canadian National or Canadian Pacific, to suit his convenience. I suggest that this principle should obtain in all agreements made by the Department of Trade and Commerce. There is no reason why a clause could not be written into such agreements to ensure that we shall enjoy the business that can be derived from the shipment of goods through Canadian ports. I have particularly in mind the situation that arose last year, and that is why I was going to ask the minister some questions in that regard. I am thinking of the statement made by the food minister in the British House of Commons last year, that, owing to the fact that the St. Lawrence had frozen, the British government were unable to ship through eastern Canadian ports in the winter months and were obliged to ship through Canadian Pacific coast ports and United States railways and ports. ests so that in future we shall not be faced with a foolish situation such as arose at that time. Perhaps be will be good enough to indicate whether such a clause as I suggest could be written into all agreements.

I wish to get some information, and at the same time to support the senior member for Halifax in what he has said in regard to the Department of Trade and Commerce regulating shipments of goods and materials they may be sending from Canada to foreign markets. I suggest that as far as possible there should be a balance in goods shipped as between port and port 'in Canada. The member for Halifax has a legitimate grievance as to the way in which that port has been used since the end of the war. During the war it was a very important port,-
And still is.

-which was cluttered up with ships from all parts of the world, and the city took a terrific beating in its efforts to accommodate war personnel and provide refuge, rations and so forth for ships from various ports. In other words, in time of war it was a handy port; since then it has been completely forgotten. Not so long ago I was in that city and I saw people cutting grass off the plot in front of the little railroad in connection with one of the piers.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Wherever you have a railroad hauling wheat you will find something growing beside it.
I am talking about the way the port has been neglected, and I think the increase in freight rates has aggravated that condition.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I am discussing foreign trade, which is the item before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Perhaps I could Shorten the discussion by saying that increases in freight rates do not apply to the export of wheat.

I am not talking about wheat at all. I am not mentioning wheat. I am referring to imports which normally would be unloaded at Halifax and shipped by rail. Ships that were partly unloaded when the new rates went into effect were taken to United States ports and came up the lakes or went to Montreal, and the result was that the eastern end of the Canadian National lost money. In my opinion it will continue to lose money as a result of that increased rate.

Can the hon. member give the details of any particular instance? I should be interested to hear them.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I have already done that in the house by questioning the minister on the strength of telegrams received from Halifax during this session. The minister already has the details of at least two ships that were affected in that way. I have not the information at my fingertips; it is in my room.
My colleague went fully into that.
I do not know anything about what the hon. gentlemen's colleague has done. If he knows the answers, he should not be asking me questions.
Read Hansard and you will see the answers.
I have already had the answers from the minister, and am not satisfied with the deal which the port of Halifax is getting.
We are glad of your support.

I do not think the senior member for Halifax is satisfied either, but I am doubtful about the junior member for that city. I am merely adding whatever weight I can to the representations of the senior member for Halifax. There is rank discrimination against that port. However, what I did get up to say was this. The department keeps elaborate statistics and turns out good information on our imports and exports. Are there any statistics in the Department of Trade and Commerce with regard to our internal trade as between province and province?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.

Perhaps there is a reason why such statistics are not kept, but I am seriously suggesting that they should be. If it is necessary for a person to ship goods from the maritimes to Vancouver, he is in the same position as if he were competing in world markets; or he may even be in a worse position. A large volume of trade flows between province and province. Different conditions exist as between province and province, and there are differences in the cost of production. The cost of marketing in the central provinces goods produced in the others is so great that it is time the government began to keep statistics with a view to achieving some kind of trade balance between one end of the country and the other.
What I see growing up in Canada is not the united nation we talk about. Greater division is setting in all the time, arising out of economic inequalities. If we are to build Canada into a nation, we must at least begin to recognize the right of every section of the country to an equal share in what we are

producing, and, as nearly as possible, to equality in income. If we do not recognize that right, before very long British Columbia and the prairie provinces will be trying to go off in one direction in order to look after themselves and the maritimes will be forced to do likewise. It has been made clear that there is no thinking in this country east of Montreal.
And none west of Fort William.

And none west of Fort William, as the hon. member says. I am sure of what I am saying about east of Montreal. No matter what comes up, it ends at Montreal. The rest of the country to the east is just held there for taxation purposes and as a base from which to operate in case of war- or that is what it looks like to me. I am not blaming the present minister. I have often felt sorry for him, because he has been chucked into every difficult problem the government has had to handle. But his shoulders are broad and I believe he is fair. If he were permitted to do as he would like to do, the situation might be different. I am asking him if it is possible, starting from now, to keep statistics as to the flow of trade between province and province. If we were getting a little booklet monthly on this subject, as we are on foreign trade, it would be a great education to hon. members and to the public generally to see just how unequal that balance of trade is as between province and province. I sometimes think we are whistling in the dark in order to keep up our courage when we talk about the united nations, government at the world level, and freedom of trade between country and country, when right here in Canada we do not have that and are not trying to get it. A good start would be the compilation of such statistics as I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
To answer the question asked by the senior member for Halifax, may I say that the Department of Trade and Commerce has an active transportation commissioner whose duty it is to see that trade is directed through Canadian ports to the greatest possible extent. The department is neither the buyer nor the seller. In ordinary commerce the buyer dictates the route by which goods will travel to market. If the traffic statistics of the port of Halifax in pre-war days are compared with those of today, I think the hon. member will find that great strides have been made in the movement of Canadian products to that port.
To reply to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I can think of no good purpose

Supply-Trade and Commerce
that would be served by considering the movement of trade over provincial boundaries. Trade is a national affair, and every effort should be made by all governments to see that no interprovincial boundaries are set up. On occasions in the past, artificial restrictions have been attempted with regard to trade crossing a provincial boundary. They have always been resisted by the federal government, and I think that is the proper course.
I believe we must regard trade in Canada as national in character rather than provincial.

I did not suggest any tariff arrangement between province and province.
I merely suggested the compilation of statistics so that we could get a look at the flow of trade between province and province-for example, on a dollar basis, the amount of goods shipped from the maritimes to Ontario and Quebec. What is coming out of those provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Coal and steel.
On a dollar basis we get back perhaps ten cents for every dollar they take in.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No. You are exporting from the maritime provinces far more than you import.
We do?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Certainly you do.
What we export is our people and raw material. It is processed up here, and then we buy it back. We export one third of Canada's basic steel, but it is processed in Ontario and Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Oh, no.
Then we buy it back.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Three-quarters of it is processed in the maritime provinces.
Where?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: At Sydney and New Glasgow.
There is no processing at Sydney at all. Sydney is just a raw material plant.

Before we leave the item relating to foreign trade, I should like to say a word with respect to trade through the port of Halifax. The minister is correct when he states that the volume of business through that port at present compares favourably with the pre-war volume of business.
So you are back to 1939.

No; we are well above 1939. But what we want to avoid is a return to the days of 1939 and those preceding. What we are interested in is to try to have as much of the maritime business as possible put through the port of Halifax. I trust that the officials to whom the minister has referred will do everything they possibly can to keep the Canadian export and import trade moving through Canadian Atlantic ports. After all, parity of rates is maintained, and exporters and importers should be urged to use Canadian channels.
My question to the hon. member for Cape Breton was prompted by the fact that he appeared to refer to the effect of the freight rate increase in diverting trade from the port of Halifax. Two instances were suggested right after the increase came into effect, in which it was alleged that these increases in rates had diverted trade from Halifax. Those cases were immediately investigated and were discussed by me and other members in this house. From the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South I presumed he had heard of other instances which have not been brought to my attention. From hjs answer to my question I realize that he was simply discussing the two cases that had been thoroughly investigated and found not to have any basis. I do not think the port of Halifax or any other port can be assisted by trying to make cases that do not exist.

The answer given by the minister in the house did not suggest there was no basis for the complaint from Halifax. Actually two ships were in process of unloading. They battened down their hatches and left; and the longshoremen's union, who were working on the job, made the complaint that, in effect, it was the result of the freight increase. I have seen editorials in Halifax papers supporting that argument. I am not a fortune-teller. But actually, two ships did pull out for the reasons I have suggested, and these are supported by the men who worked on the job. At the time, the minister said it was not because of the freight rate increase. Hon. members may accept that statement if they wish. I am still doubtful. I do not doubt the minister's word, but I would think there was a real reason for the ships leaving Halifax harbour at that time.

This item refers to commercial relations and foreign tariffs division, including a contribution of $2,800 to the international customs tariffs bureau. There has been a complete change in the set-up of the department. This is a practically new division. If we turn to page 251 of the estimates we

Supply-Trade and Commerce
find the details for this item. This new division deals with tariffs and exports, and in my view it upsets the whole policy of the department as it has operated since confederation. As to the reference in the item to the international customs tariffs bureau, I say that is where our trouble started-over at Geneva, with these foreign bureaux. Trade in grain and cattle used to flow east and west to the overseas market of the world. Now, however, because of these Geneva pacts, a great change in exports and imports has been made, and this new division has been created. We are upsetting the whole trade and commerce of this country as it has operated since confederation, and this change has come from Geneva. Trade and commerce is the lifeblood of this country. Under former ministers and the present one we have become the fifth trading nation of the world. The department has done excellent work, but our trade commissioners throughout the world have been duplicated most unnecessarily by those from other departments.
The businessmen and working class depend upon trade for their work. I do not believe in the department's new policy of going all over the world and arranging new divisions. I say that all this trouble started in the international customs union. I believe our trade agents throughout the world have done good work. One has only to visit the international trade fair to realize the truth of that statement. I hope those who did not see the fair the Saturday before last will see it tomorrow, because that is the last day. The trade fair is housed in the coliseum which was built by the city. The government has helped to the extent of only $100,000 for a trade and commerce building at the exhibition grounds. The city of Toronto has spent nearly $30,000,000, of its own volition for ground buildings and permanent exhibits; it received only a small grant.

Following what has been said by the hon. member for Broadview, hon. members must have been chagrined to read in the press last night that there had been some criticism of the international trade fair by some of the exhibitors from Great Britain.
I believe hon. members who attended were more than pleased and gratified with the exhibits and the progress the various exhibitors told us they were making. I am not for one moment attempting to foment criticism, but I would ask the minister to see that investigation be made or some attention given to the complaints, and an answer made to those who, in a way, have tried to pour cold water on the benefits which, as I believe all 
hon. members will agree, have resulted from the international trade fair.
Some time ago we were told in the press that the fair would be held again next year. I should like to hear some cheering words from the minister about the fair held this year, and I suggest that the rumours that the fair has not been a success should be quashed.
The publication "Foreign Trade," put out early last year by the Department of Trade and Commerce, has been well received by industry and commerce in Canada. In my own constituency of Parkdale I have sent out a great number of issues of this publication. I know that one person, who was engaged in the forwarding and shipping business, sending goods to all parts of Canada and to Great Britain, found the publication of such great interest that he immediately communicated with all the trade commissioners appointed by Canada, and by so doing has made a direct contact for business to flow to those various countries.
A few moments ago the minister said that he had an active transportation commissioner here in Canada, but he also pointed out that the buyer is the one who dictates the route by which goods are shipped, I am satisfied from my own experience in business that industry in Canada does not know the routes, and does not know the way it should be shipping goods. I am pleased to know that the publication to which I refer has had the effect of informing the public to some extent as to how they should go about it. If I might offer a suggestion, I would say the department should find ways and means of placing in the publication further information respecting transport.
Most of the people engaged in industry are looking for new markets abroad. As some of our markets in some of the sterling area countries seem to be drying up, our trade commissioners, who have done a good job, should make their positions just that much more active. We live by trade in Canada; it is the backbone of our country, and we must back up this particular branch of our Department of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Referring to the trade fair, let me say that there are about 1,500 exhibitors, representing most of the nations of the world. Of that number, many are doing good business, while others are not. That is bound to be so.
I have talked to a good many exhibitors and, by and large, they are happy about the fair and intend to return next year. But there are those whose goods are priced out of line and they are not able to sell them. I understand that that is true of a few English firms.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The real test of the fair will come next year when we see how many exhibitors of this year will pay the fees for the privilege of exhibiting next year. All the information we have now is that the fair next year will be even more successful.
Is it intended that the fair shall be an annual event?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We are going to hold the trade fair next year, anyway.

I think we all appreciate the significance of the trade fair. I want to thank the minister for his invitation to attend the opening ceremonies and view the exhibits. It was a unique opportunity to see the products of various countries. I believe that much good will come from it, inasmuch as those who are exhibiting will have an opportunity to become better acquainted with the products and the producers of other countries.
With the hon. member for Parkdale, I think that this is one department of government with which we should all be most vitally concerned. Canada is a tremendous producing country. Probably we would have a better appreciation of our productive capacity if we looked back at the production during the war. If we are to survive we must cultivate the old markets and seek new and greater ones. I am glad to see the interest that is being taken in maintaining and possibly improving our present position. We produce far more than we can consume, and we must have an outlet for our surplus products.
There is a matter I want to discuss which is related to this item but which runs through all the various items of this department and of others. Perhaps the minister can give an explanation which will serve to answer for all. I am referring to the items for temporary assistance. In this item there is an amount of $49,551 for temporary assistance, while the total for all the items for the department is upwards of $1,500,000. What I am anxious to find out is how these people are employed and what qualifications they must have. Are they under the civil service? How 'are their appointments made? What is the average period of their employment? Are they seasonal employees? Why is this item of temporary assistance in every estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
At the moment the department has a total of 3,447 employees, of whom 449 of the staff in Ottawa and 760 of the staff outside of Ottawa are permanent. The temporary staff in Ottawa amounts to 1,413, of which 1,091 are in the bureau of statistics. My hon. friend will appreciate that the work of the bureau fluctuates. When the bureau is
taking a census there is a big expansion, and in between times the requirements are for fewer employees. Aside from that I do not think the proportions are out of line with those of the other departments.
I could not say how long some of these temporaries have been employed. My hon. friend will appreciate the fact that during the war the Department of Munitions and Supply and the Department of Reconstruction and Supply were temporary departments and all the employees were temporary. The practice of this department is not any different from that of the other departments in the division between permanent and temporary employees.
I do not suggest that the temporaries in the minister's department are out of line with those in other departments. Are these temporaries full-time employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: They are full-time employees appointed by the civil service commission, in the same way as other employees, but they have not obtained permanent status.

Can the minister tell us more about the system? Does the civil service commission or the department recommend the appointments? In this case the salaries of the permanent employees total approximately $39,000, while those of the temporary assistants total $49,551. Apparently there are not many persons involved, because I imagine that those with permanent status would be relatively few. I take it their salaries would be the higher of the two classifications. There must be a large number of persons in the $49,000 group. Do they have to be with the department a year? What is the system? This all seems rather odd; one would not find it in any other type of business with which the minister is familiar outside of government administration. I should think the temporary nature of the employment must have some effect on the morale of the workers, particularly if they are kept on year after year on a temporary basis. If their morale is affected, that in turn affects the work and efficiency of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
When any person enters the public service he does so as a temporary, and there is a minimum requirement of one year's service before he can be made permanent. Usually more time than that is allowed to elapse before he is made permanent. The example to which the hon. member has referred is a new branch. In the import division there are 45 employees, of whom seven have been made permanent and 38 are temporary. As the branch grows older,
Supply-Trade and Commerce

more permanent positions will be established and more temporaries will be moved into those positions.

I believe it is the foreign trade services vote we are dealing with at the moment. There is nothing out of line there in the ratio of permanent and temporary employees; in fact it is rather in favour of permanent employees in comparison with other items having to do with the Department of Trade and Commerce. I want to find out if there is any hard and fast system which might keep only ten per cent of employees on a temporary basis, as is done in the post office, or do the employees know where they stand when they seek a position with the department? Surely there is some system.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is the system that applies to the whole public service. A man enters as a temporary, and after a certain time when positions are set up
How long?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The system is pretty well operated by the civil service commission. As a matter of fact when a man enters the employ of the department he is under the direction of the civil service commission. At a certain time his status is changed from temporary to permanent.
If it is a certain time, it is not an uncertain time; what is the time?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: A minimum of one year.
That is most uncertain. The minister appreciates the significance of my question?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: He certainly would have to wait a year, anyway.

Can the minister say how many of the temporary employees included in the $49,000 item have been there less than one year, and how many have been there three years? Can he give me some indication of the length of time they have been serving in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend is discussing the commercial relations and foreign tariffs division, vote 441?
The vote we are on now. It is a small item.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I was looking at the import division when I gave the other figure. There are 28 employees in the commercial relations branch, of whom 12 are permanent and 16 are temporary. I think my hon. friend will find that the salaries are in about the same proportion.

I am surprised to know that, because one would think that the permanent employees would be the senior men and would get substantially more than
the temporaries. Surely positions commanding salaries, for instance, of $4,800 and $3,400. should be entitled to permanent status after a reasonable length of time during which it can be determined whether their services are satisfactory and they can pass the required examination. I again ask the minister if he knows how long these sixteen temporary assistants have served, how many have served one year, how many have served two or three years, and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Four or five have been taken on in the last few months. I would have to get the individual records of each person to give my hon. friend the information he wants.

There is a minimum requirement of one year's service as a temporary before an employee can be made permanent, and the only certainty in the department seems to be the uncertainty as to how long a person must work as a temporary before he is made permanent. This item comes up time after time in the estimates, and I think we should know exactly what the situation is. Surely after one year's service a man would have demonstrated whether he was efficient enough for permanent status.

The minister did not enlighten us on the question I put. If he is sometimes disgusted with the operations of parliament he should remember that members may be disgusted when they cannot get the information they seek. We still do not know what the system is as to making temporaries permanent. All the minister has told us is that there is a list of temporary employees, and in this particular branch, in relation to the small number of employees which I took as an example, he said that five or six came in during the year. I know nothing about the others, whether three or four of them have served for two or for three years, or what not. If the minister would be co-operative I am sure he would find that the committee would be co-operative with him.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is hardly the job of the minister to move civil servants around. That is the job of the civil service commission and the personnel officer of the department. My hon. friend picks out a group of fifteen people and asks why they are not made permanent. Perhaps they do not want to become permanent. A great many girls in the civil service are not the slightest bit interested in permanency or in a pension. I can tell my hon. friend that because I know of cases that prove my point. A case came up the other day of a man who had been fifty-one years in one branch, and was still a temporary, because he prefered to be a temporary. I do not know how I can explain the inner thoughts of a group of civil servants whom I do not know personally. My hon. friend has been here a long time, and no doubt has been in contact with the civil service commission. It is not a matter of some general rule. If it were, I could explain the rule to him. It is a matter of the individual's wishes, and not knowing the individuals, I cannot give my hon. friend the information he wants.

The average salary is $3,000, and not many of these would be in the classification the minister mentioned. If it is the wish of the employee himself that he be not put on a permanent basis, very well; we have got something. If there is a limit of one year's temporary service, has the department
Supply-Trade and Commerce

recommended the permanent appointment of every employee in this little section who has been there one year and who has fully proved himself? Does the commission wait for the recommendation of the head of the department? If the head of the department has not recommended for permanency an efficient civil servant who has been there for one year, why has he not done so?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
If we are satisfied that the employee intends to make a career of the public service, usually he is made permanent.
If we are not satisfied that he intends to make a permanent job of it, or if we are not satisfied that he can fill his particular niche to the satisfaction of the department in the long run, he is not made permanent. That is about the size of it.

There is another item which recurs all through these estimates, namely, sundries, to which I referred yesterday. In this department it amounts to about $160,000, or 1-25 per cent of the total estimates of the department. It seems to me that these are excessive expenses which cannot be specified at the time the estimates are made up. I am beginning to think that instead of having a sundry item for each division or branch of the department, there should be a sundry item for the department itself. This sundry item for the whole department should be under the control of the minister or the deputy minister. Here we have one and a quarter per cent of all the estimates of this department indicated as sundries. I think it should be under one heading.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I think the officers of the department would be all for what my hon. friend suggests, the big blanket item, but I do not think it would be as good for the treasury as it is to have the sundry items limited to small amounts in each particular branch.
It is the small amounts that make the big amount in the end.

I want to say a word about the trade fair. I think the minister will find that the people who were not able to sell goods at the trade fair were from countries whose currencies were overpriced in terms of world currency. I think that is the main reason.
The very great success of the trade fair was in no small measure due to the officials who staffed it. I should like to pay tribute to Colonel Orme Barrett and the officials who worked under him so effectively for the success of this fair and of the accompanying "world trade week."

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Since the subject has been brought up I should like to say that we have a splendid group of officials in charge, of the fair. Mr. Bannerman, and his assistant, Mr. Dayton, took the fair in hand with very little to work on. The success of the arrangements and the success of the fair in general are both due to the zeal and imagination that they have put into the project.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
442. Export division, $197,564.

I noticed in the press the day before yesterday that 3,000 pounds of flour had been seized on an Italian ship in Montreal harbour. Was it seized because these people were unable to get an export permit? The Royal Canadian Mounted Police stepped in, seized the flour and demanded $400 as a penalty or a fine, and said there would be further charges. Is it difficult to get a permit to ship flour out of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes, it is very difficult to get a permit. Flour and wheat are under strict international allocation. Anyone who could buy flour in the domestic market and export it might reap a handsome reward, perhaps double his money, and, in doing so, deprive the farmer of participation in the export price, or rather the world price of the product. I do not know the circumstances of this particular shipment, but I would judge that it was wheat bought in the domestic market and sent into export channels without a permit.

The article said that the flour was bought in local stores in Montreal; therefore they evidently knew that they could not get a permit. I wanted to find out if the department had strict control over that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.

Item 442 and the items following it amount to an expenditure of almost $3,000,000. The items are divided into export division, import division, industrial development division, trade commissioner service, and so on. I want to ask the minister first the general question as to how this whole thing is organized. I have in mind the debate which took place on the passing of the export-import bill a year ago. I formed a great respect for some of the officials who were dealing with that. I want to know just how this shapes up in the minister's mind. We passed the export-import bill a year ago, the duration of which was roughly a year. It was extended this year. I should like to have the minister give us first information as to the likely duration of this. I am not asking him to predict how many months or years it

Supply-Trade and Commerce
will last; I am asking him to give us a picture of the kind of trading world we are in at the moment, and in particular the relation between this export and import branch and our trade commissioners all over the world. Are the export and import branches purely controlling branches? Are they merely prohibiting this or that, or are they actually entering into and controlling business?
I want to give the minister an illustration of what happened before the committee. He will know of the kind of thing I have in mind. A year ago we had this illustration which interested me very much. It was pointed out there had to be certain export controls on steel. It was also pointed out that the department was exercising a discretion as to the kind of business which would be allowed an export licence-that is to say, businesses which they thought would be more likely to continue after the reconstruction period were given export licences. On the other hand, those that they thought had less expectation of going on were denied export licences. I mention this only as an illustration of the fact that these controls seem to be entering very largely into the whole course of business.
I recognize the fact that we are living in a world where controls are in the atmosphere. To sum up, I ask the minister to give us in this connection, as I asked last night, a comprehensive picture of the import and export situation. Will he illustrate by saying that certain commodities are restricted, and tell us just how it enters into the whole fabric of the business community? What is the course at the present time? Are things tightening up? Is there less freedom or more? Finally, will the minister state as specifically as he can the relationship between these three organizations, if they are three organizations, namely, import, export and trade commissioners? I take it these are the people who are seeking business all over the world for our exporters.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend is going outside the foreign trade services. He is talking about the import permit division.
I thought we were on item 442.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Yes, but it does not include the licensing division. If the hon. member will look at item 462 he will see that that section deals with the export permit branch. These are all promotional branches. Item 441 is concerned with furnishing information on tariffs; item 442 promotes exports from within Canada, and item 443 promotes imports into
Canada-that is through men working in Canada to promote imports. Item 444 has to do with the industrial development division.
Yes.
We have not come to that yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No. Item 445 has to do with trade commissioner service, trade commissioners located in different countries. Item 446 has to do with trade publicity and advertising in Canada and abroad. We can discuss the licensing division on item 440 when we return to it.

I accept the minister's correction. I did not observe item 462, but I now ask the minister this question. As I understand it, item 442, the export division, has to do with a group of people working in Canada to promote export trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That is correct.

I can understand trade commissioners working abroad to promote export trade. I think I understand the nature of their functions. I do not think I understand fully the functions of those covered by 442. Perhaps the minister will explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The trade commissioner reports on the requirements for a certain commodity in South Africa, let us say, or Australia, or some other country. That comes to the department and it is sent to the branch we are now discussing. That branch gets in touch with appropriate manufacturers and says, "We have a market for this commodity; can you supply it?" Information goes back to the trade commissioner that it can be supplied by a certain firm or firms. The branch is simply a- link between the trade commissioner and those desiring to export from this country.
Would that be small firms who do not themselves maintain a selling staff abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Even firms who do maintain staffs abroad are glad to get the help of the trade commissioner service. It is available to every firm in Canada. It is the business of this branch to know Canadian industry and to know what parts of Canadian industry would be interested in inquiries abroad for certain items.

Who heads this particular
division?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Mr. Bull.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
There are certain products for which we are finding it difficult to get a market. May I discuss the export of apples and tobacco under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I suppose so.

We can now produce more tobacco in Canada than we can use domestically, and therefore there is an exportable surplus. The English market is pretty well shut off at present, by reason of their austerity program, I presume. I understand an effort has been made to find other markets, but I would like to know whether England might be in a position to import some of our surplus tobacco this year. The minister was good enough to meet a delegation and discuss the matter with them, but I do not know whether any further information is available. Has England indicated whether she will import Canadian tobacco this year, or are other markets available for our surplus?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not think there is anything to add to what the tobacco industry has been tdld. We are working on the problem, but there is no indication as yet that we shall be able to sell Canadian tobacco to England. However, the door is not closed, and we hope that sales will be possible.
Has the department made inquiries to find out whether other countries might be interested in our surplus Canadian tobacco?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Every trade commissioner has been advised that Canada is likely to have a surplus of tobacco for export, and all trade commissioners are working on it.

A special effort should be made along this line, because there is a great deal of submarginal land that could be used for growing tobacco. This would bring under cultivation many areas that have not been able to produce a great deal in the past. It would be to the advantage of various counties in this province and other parts of Canada as well where tobacco can be grown. I urge that every effort be made to find a market for our surplus tobacco.
I would also like to ask what the situation is [DOT]as regards apples. I understand there is a surplus in Canada. Is there a possibility of finding a market for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We are aware of the importance of tobacco and are making an effort to sell it. We have sold every tobacco crop so far, and we hope to sell this crop. As far as apples are concerned, we are taking care of the situation in every part of the land. The 1947 crop in British Columbia has been wholly sold.
Wholly sold?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
There are 600,000 boxes still in Yale.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I have definite information that the crop is sold.
Perhaps the minister could check that up.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am giving the information.
I was asking if the minister would check it up.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I have the information and I am giving it. The crops in other parts of the country have been taken care of, with the help of the government. We are doing all we can about the apple crop. The British market is closed to Canadian apples. The domestic crop in Britain is considerable and the United Kingdom government does not permit importation of apples. The United States tariffs have been lowered, and every effort will be made to sell apples in that country. A good proportion of the British Columbia crop was sold in Brazil under a barter arrangement for oranges, which was worked out with the help of the department. We are exploring every possibility of exchanging apples either for dollars or for some other saleable commodity.

As for apples being sold, I think it might be well for the department to ascertain whether they have been sold, because in my part of the county they have been finding it difficult to get a market. They had to peddle them around in the various cities to get rid of them, putting them up *in special packages. There were apples in my county for which a market could not be found.

A good many fowl are exported from my district to the United States. I had occasion last week to get a permit for one of our shippers and he was held off for a week. There were 10,000 birds in stock that had to be fed. I presume this comes under the export permit branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
It is really under 442. We have not yet come to that. However, the department issues export permits for fowl, with the advice of the Department of Agriculture. This department exercises no discretion in the matter. We simply take the advice of the Department of Agriculture. The export of live fowl is under permit, and we regulate exports in consultation with the United States Department of Agriculture.

Just now they are cutting down on the granting of permits, so they say. This firm could not get one for about ten days. This small firm say that they are giving them to large packers. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not know.
If you give them to large packers you should give them to the small ones too, because you should treat all the people in the same way in the export of these birds.

speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that if we are giving export permits, the small man gets them first.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a matter that I pointed out to the Minister of Agriculture some time ago. I refer to the shipping of gift apples to Britain. Before the war we sent large quantities of apples as gifts from British Columbia. The apples were exported for delivery to the persons designated. They were sent to Great Britain in bulk or carload lots, and then delivered by carrier to the person designated. The British ministry of food will not accept them unless they are consigned to the ministry direct, and they are allowed to designate where those apples shall go. The fruit organizations in British Columbia are confident that they could ship this year in the neighbourhood of half a million boxes of apples to Great Britain as gift apples, a direct contribution of the Canadian people, by putting on a campaign in co-operation with the Canadian Legion, women's organizations and farmers' organizations. But they cannot organize a campaign because of the present restrictions imposed by the British ministry of food. I ask the minister if something cannot be done to discuss this matter with the British ministry of food so that this half million boxes of apples can go forward. It is a matter of particular concern to some of the fruit growers in my constituency who for years have been growing two particular varieties of apples for the English market. I refer to Cox's Orange and Jonathan. Owing to the loss of the British preference, unless something is done in this respect the Cox's Orange growers will simply not have any income this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend will understand that the Canadian government is doing nothing to interfere with the sending of gift boxes of apples to England. This government has discussed the subject with the British ministry of food, who have explained the problems surrounding the situation and have not acceded to the Canadian request for consideration. I think there is a good deal of reason behind their refusal to do so. Therefore I can offer little hope that the British ministry will change its position.

In connection with trade commissioner service there is an item here of 1366,000 for permanent help. I want to relate that to an item lower down, living allowances, $476,000; and to another one further down, cost of living bonus abroad, $56,000. These items look disproportionate, but there may be sound reasons behind them. In fact I have known cases in which foreign trade representatives have been underpaid in relation to the job they were called upon to do. Will the minister explain how it is that a group of trained men of standing who get $366,000 require $476,000 for living allowances? Are the living allowances tax free, or are they partly to allow for inflation, which latter item I suppose is covered by the cost-of-living bonus abroad? In other words are these foreign trade officers, to whom I suppose the item largely relates, paid anything like an adequate salary, or is it necessary for them to get a cost-of-living bonus in other countries? Surely the cost of living in the various countries to which they are assigned cannot be so much higher than it is in Canada. Yet the ordinary salary does not seem to be adequate. As to cost-of-living bonuses where there may be inflation, there is a smaller item of $56,000. Would the minister explain generally why those items are disproportionate?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The salaries of trade commissioners are based on the Canadian cost of living. The cost of living varies greatly in other countries. For instance, I am told that in Caracas a stenographer gets $400 a month, and that is consistent with the scale of living in Caracas.
What kind of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
United States dollars. We have prevailing today an uneven situation throughout the world with respect to the cost of living, and it is necessary to adjust the living allowances accordingly. The bonuses relate to the help that is employed abroad. That is, in Egypt bonuses are paid to Egyptians who are employed in our service. The allowances are made after careful survey by the dominion bureau of statistics as to a proper adjustment which in the specified country would give a salary-plus allowance which would be equivalent to the salary alone in Canada at the rate indicated.

It seems extraordinary that the allowances would require to be nearly 150 per cent more than the salaries themselves. After all, these people are not called upon to maintain large establishments. They are business representatives. I have certain fears on one point, and I should like to be reassured. Are they paid a salary which is commensurate with the position they must maintain abroad to do the work which the department expects them to do? If the answer is in the negative, does the minister expect that in the future, as the world becomes more stabilized-as we hope it will in short order-this item will almost entirely disappear?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate the difficulty of fixing a man's salary on the basis of the fact that he happens to be stationed for the time being at Buenos Aires. We could adjust his salary so that he could live properly in Buenos Aires, consistent with his situation in that country. But we prefer to fix his salary based on his living in Canada, and make such adjustment by way of bonus as the temporary situation warrants. I think my hon. friend will agree that is a sounder method. If we move the man to a country where the difference in the cost of living is not great, he would get a small allowance. But if he happened to be moved to a country such as the one I mentioned, namely, Caracas-which I believe is the extreme situation today-he would need a much larger living allowance. We believe the salaries are reasonable for the position, provided the cost of living is the same as in Canada.
I suppose the living allowances are tax free?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
I must say this indicates that Canada deserves some credit for the fact that the cost of living in this country is so much lower than that which prevails in other areas.

1,1,1,. Industrial development division, $27,863.

I am sure that with his great knowledge of industry the minister will have an opportunity here to do one of his big jobs. The vote of course is small, and it is possible that the work has not yet got well under way. The promotion of industrial development is one activity in which the minister has had a good deal of experience, and I am sure he will do a good job. I should imagine, however, that the division would have to work differently from the manner in which it now works.
Perhaps in this connection a leaf could be taken out of the program of the Toronto industrial commission, an organization with which I am sure the minister is familiar. They have done a masterful job in promoting industry in that city. The commission was organized in 1929 by the private effort of gentlemen in Toronto who were interested in the growth of the city's industrial activities. Since that time many promoters of industry, including myself, have been greatly pleased with the work they have done.
The commission in Toronto has brought to the Toronto district 264 businesses, both large and small, now employing directly about 16,000 employees. That is a large number of men and women to be furnished employment and to be kept occupied. The sum of $45,000,000 has been invested in new capital, and these new business ventures occupy about 6,000,000 square feet of floor space.
With the small amount of money at its disposal, this division of the minister's department will not be able to do a great deal. I learned recently from an old country industrialist that no less than a thousand industries of one kind or another plan to come to America. Naturally, if it is possible to get them, we want most of those industries to come to Canada, and to open up business in the various provinces.
The Toronto industrial commission, when submitting information to an industrialist who is considering coming to Ontario, follows certain lines which I suggest might well be followed in all the provinces. They try to present to the industrialist the advantages of Toronto as a great railway centre, favourably situated so far as highways, airways, and shipping are concerned. They explain carefully the facility with which raw products can
Supply-Trade and Commerce

be brought to that city for fabrication. Many centres in Canada have raw products right at their doors.
The Toronto commission attempts to present the desirability of living in a city like Toronto, with its educational facilities, the beauties of the surrounding country, a ready market, and other important features. They also say that we have cheap power.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: At times you do.

As the minister knows, the present condition is only temporary. No one knows that better than the minister. We have expanded our power requirements by leaps and bounds, until today I believe the provincial hydro commission is selling around three to four million horsepower of electric energy a year. That is a tremendous amount of power. There is no doubt that the province will soon overcome its temporary power shortage. Within a year or more they will be connecting their wires to another million and a half horsepower. There may be a shortage even after that-indeed, I hope industrial development is such that there will be. In the next year we should have five or six million horsepower available, and I should like to see industry grow to a point where we would require seven or eight million.
I should like to see this division make those representations to prospective industrialists. They Should point out that power is available. Indeed, if the program I enunciated on April 25 for producing power in the maritime provinces is carried through, to produce power out of coal, they too will be in a position to provide cheaper power facilities for new industry.
The vote would indicate that at present the division is a small one. However, no one knows better than I do the capacity of the minister to bring industry here-and I give him credit for it. I am not one who censures him. I know his 'capacity, and I believe the division should be expanded so that it could bring to Canada the greater portion of the thousand industrialists who will move from the old country, France and Czechoslovakia to America.
I look forward to this country having a population of 25,000,000. I may not live to see that day, but we have incomparable resources, we have great potential power developments, and there are great advantages here. I feel sure that this branch could be expanded to do a wonderful job, just as the Toronto industrial commission has done with its limited facilities. Other cities and towns have industrial commissions, but I am not wholly familiar with them. I support the minister and urge him to expand this division.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend. I might say that the merger of the Department 
of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Reconstruction and Supply will make it possible greatly to strengthen this division. The committee will be aware that the work of the department of reconstruction is to stimulate industry, create new industries and facilitate the changing of war industries into permanent industries. The men engaged in that work are still in the department of reconstruction, but we hope the merger will have taken place within the next year, after which we would hope to have a much stronger industrial development division.

I am happy to hear what the minister has just said, and I support what the hon. member for Davenport has said about this division. I think what the hon. member has said is in accordance with what we in this group .have advocated for years, in fact it is part of our program. There is a need for a commission or board which would plan the development of the resources of this country from coast to coast. With a disintegrated economy we have the development, on the one hand, of things which we do not need, and a lack of development, on the other hand, of resources which would balance our economy.
I notice that this vote is only for $27,863. That would, seem to indicate that the only service that could be rendered would be the diffusion of information to industrial firms. As we go into the post-war period I think an industrial commission should be set up in order that our people may have the benefits of the resources of this country. We are penalizing our people by placing restrictions on imports because of a shortage of United States dollars. We import coal from the United States to the amount of $225 million, or about one-quarter of our deficit of United States dollars. If we had a reasonable and imaginative program to develop our coal resources we could largely offset our deficit of United States dollars. In addition, as the hon. member for Davenport has pointed out, there should be a further development of our power and other resources.
Does this division have anything to do with the establishment of new industry, particularly in the west, where processing industries of many kinds could be set up?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If anyone desired information as to the potentialities of a particular area, that would be provided by this division. The type of work mentioned by my hon. friend would foe carried on by the department of reconstruction.

By the different departments? Then from that the people of Canada ought to be able to get an idea of the amounts paid. Does the publication give the number of employees and the amount of salary that was paid to them, say last month?

The minister has stated that very confidently, but I find it difficult to believe that he is right. First of all, let me say I have great respect for the bureau of statistics and for Mr. Marshall in particular. I have found him

most helpful and co-operative. I found to my great surprise that I could not get from him a complete list of the government employees, and he was frank in saying that he could not give it to me. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I shall be very glad to send for the publication, mark it, and send it across to my hon. friend. The reason the question cannot be answered easily is that hon. members ask questions which never coincide with what is actually published. I am told that we publish the numbers of all people regularly employed in the civil service, but not in crown companies or in various branches. We state how many employees are permanent and how many are temporary. We state the total salaries paid during the month. That is published each month. I shall be glad to get the publication and send it to my thon. friends. The questions asked in the house are not as simple as that. Hon. members ask for other data which require compilation.

If this was merely the result of questions I put down on paper, I would not have the same objection; but what I am talking about is the result of several conversations with Mr. Marshall. The result was we got to the point where he told me the figures were not available. I was not able to get any figures that I could use at the time I wanted them. I am not criticizing Mr. Marshall-quite the contrary.

The minister said that the questions which are asked are not asked in the way in which the figures are kept. The point is that the information which the member asks for is no good to him three months after the question is asked. I asked a question as to the number of employees on such and such a date, say December 31 of last year. The reply I received gave the number to December 15 last year, or whatever date suited them, and did not give the general picture. Like the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, I have tried time and time again to find out how many employees there are in the government of Canada, how many in the C.B.C., and so on, but I never could find out. I should be glad to have the publication sent to me, too.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I am not so much concerned with the question whether the employees are permanent or temporary as I am with the possibility of getting the number reduced so that there can be some relief for the taxpayers.
