I do not wish to take up a great deal of time on this matter now, although I feel it is a most important one, especially for the particular area from which I come. I am not criticizing in any way, shape or form. With the staff available, and the facilities they have for handling this large business, as it is at the present time, I think the bureau is doing a good job. In a speech in the house here some time ago it was suggested, I think by the hon. member for Lambton West, that a separate department should be set up. Later on, speaking on the same subject, I myself suggested a commission. I fully realize that this is a big job. I want to pay tribute to Mr. Leo Dolan, director of the travel bureau, who is serving this country well, not only in his operations in this country but in all his travels. I think he is doing a marvellous job for us wherever he goes. Recently I think he did a magnificent job in going to the United States when we were having a little bit of difficulty with our exchange problem, and when we were being threatened with a boycott of money coming into Canada. I followed that matter up, and I think Mr. Dolan did a grand job there. He was able to overcome many difficulties.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
However, I still have a strong feeling that with the amount of work which comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce this is a big item to come under its jurisdiction, unless there could be some way of setting up a commission or at least a commissioner. 11 Mr. Dolan carried with him a title similar to that of deputy minister, I think it would be of great advantage to him in approaching the people of other countries, and would pay off well in Canada. Not only that, but it would give him an approach when meeting provincial and other governments.
Coming back to the actual department, it would seem to me, that if he were in a position of more power to carry this message to the people about this important business, it would be something worthwhile to this country. I make that as a constructive suggestion, and not in any other way. Is the department giving any consideration to methods whereby this great industry of ours will be taken care of, by possibly giving it more stress and placing it in a position of greater importance than it has occupied in the past?
I have gone into this matter of advertising. I looked up all the different magazines and the different methods of advertising our country and I do not know that I have so much criticism with regard to that matter. But I make the suggestion that a personal contact, either through Mr. Dolan or an assistant to him, in other countries, would be worth a good deal. I believe one personal contact with a group of businessmen in those respective communities is worth a great deal more than advertising that will cost considerably more money. I feel that there is nothing like personal contact when it comes to advertising our goods. Therefore I would make that suggestion; and I should like to have the minister, if he will, comment on it at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The activities of the federal government in the field of tourism, as my hon. friend will appreciate, are confined to only one agency, which is intended to be a coordinating one and to supplement the work being done by the nine provinces, whose expenditures run into considerably more money in the aggregate than is spent by the federal government. We feel that Mr. Dolan is running a most aggressive department. We think he is drawing tourists to Canada. It will be the constant effort of the department to strengthen the branch.

First of all, I should like to commend the department, and Mr. Dolan as well, for the work that has been done. One of the things that would help the tourist traffic in Canada more than anything else,
especially in my own city, is in connection with the increase in the limit to $400 in the amount of goods a United States person may take back with him. I might point out to the minister that the tourist will not buy in Canada fine luggage and things of that kind that they can take back, because they will not pay the 25 per cent excise tax. If the government will remove that tax on things of that kind, they will increase the tourist trade. They would do more good by taking many of these taxes off, which are not necessary now anyway, than by any other method I know of, and their removal would certainly help the tourist trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I might as well set my hon. friend right. There is no excise tax on goods bought in Canada for export.
But people take them back, individually.
Do they get a refund of the excise tax when they take them back?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: They have it delivered to them.
I was not referring to having it delivered.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is cheaper to do it the other way.
They want to take it with them.

I am sure hon. members would like to have some expression from the minister respecting the repeated suggestions since 1945 by those who are interested in the tourist industry. Those suggestions have varied from that of having a separate ministry to having a commission which would work in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities, and also the suggestion to have a deputy minister in charge of the tourist industry.
We know that in Ontario they have a new department for that purpose, and I believe in Quebec the tourist industry is under the supervision of the premier. From time to time it has been pointed out in the house by hon. members on both sides that it is important to develop this industry. I have suggested repeatedly that a separate ministry be considered. Before I proceed further with my questions, would the minister be prepared to advise the committee whether or not any change is contemplated or has been under consideration? After he has completed what he has to say, I should like to continue.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not think the government ever considered appointing a minister for tourist traffic. It seems to me that the overhead of the ministry might be more than the expenditures. We now have a tourist branch, and the head of that branch has all the authority he requires. We have recently given him a senior assistant, the purpose being to free him to do more travelling in countries which are the source of our tourist business. So far as I know, he has no difficulty in working with other provinces of the dominion. I have attended conferences at which he has presided, and it seems to me that his position there is quite assured. I cannot imagine any step which would make his position any stronger. If hon. members think the best executive organization is a commission, they are entitled to their opinion. I have never shared that view. I believe a director is much more efficient, so far as organizing the tourist industry is concerned.

I appreciate the minister's frankness. I am wondering, however, if the government appreciates the possibilities of the tourist industry. Figures concerning the industry are quite revealing when one remembers that the administration of it is not on a departmental level. For that reason I have maintained that it is entitled to more consideration than it has been given. We know that in some countries the tourist industry is a large one. I am told that in Switzerland it runs to about a billion dollars a year, and we know that in the United States it is much greater than the difference between the population of the United States and that of Canada would indicate.
We are not getting what we can get of United States money, which we need so badly. It has been only within the last two or three years that the tourist industry has been discussed with the provinces, and no doubt some good has come from those discussions. I was not suggesting that the director be appointed a deputy minister. I was .more concerned with some change which would increase our tourist industry to the point which I think this country should have.
Perhaps I might illustrate what I have in mind. Under the present set-up, we shall suppose a representation is made to develop the tourist industry. Let us suppose that it is recommended that a boat basin or well be cleaned out on a stream emptying into lake Huron. The only reason for clearing the sand bar would be to permit yachts and pleasure craft coming in from Detroit. If they were able to use the harbour they would probably spend two or three hundred thousand dollars a year in that area. Would representations

be made through his department, if any association wished to undertake that work so as to bring United States dollars to this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
An application of that kind would be made to the Department of Public Works, although it might come through the director of the tourist industry. As my hon. friend knows, the Department of Public Works is charged with the responsibility of developing harbours.
However, I do not think the difficulty in Canada is in getting the numbers of tourists, because the numbers are satisfactory. Our difficulty is that we have not the resorts or other attractions which would induce the tourist to stay here to spend his money in Canada. When we were free to travel to the United States, although our numbers were small when compared with the numbers who came from the United States to Canada, our total expenditures in the United States for holiday purposes were about half the total expenditure by United States tourists in Canada. I agree with the hon. member that further developments should be made in connection with tourist accommodation and tourist attractions.

I certainly agree with what the minister says with respect to accommodation, or lack of it, for United States tourists. No language could be too strong to impress upon those who cater to the tourists that they must do their part to see that good food and proper lodging are accorded. I believe that in the last fifteen years there has not been $100,000 spent for tourist accommodation all the way from Windsor to Ottawa; yet they clamour for tourists. I would take this opportunity to say to those who are interested in the promotion of the tourist industry, by way of giving accommodation, that they are not doing their share. I have in mind particularly hotels and restaurants, and other facilities for tourist accommodation.
What plans has the government further to integrate this work with the work of the provinces and municipalities in the promotion of this industry? Then, has the government considered developing the industry by offering accommodation in the nature of fields for the landing of aircraft throughout the various areas in Canada; and what further plans has the government with respect to the Trans-Canada highway?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
My. hon. friend has covered a good deal of territory. For the last two years we have held an interprovincial conference for the discussion of the tourist traffic.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
At that conference the plans of all the provinces, the transportation, bus and steamship companies are laid on the table. It is presided over by the head of the federal bureau. Plans are co-ordinated, and suggestions are made wherever they can be strengthened. So far as I know, there is a continuous effort to improve our tourist industry in Canada, and to strengthen it.

Has the department under consideration any plan for the exchange of films with the United States? It occurred to me that perhaps through some form of barter we could have our films shown in the United States with a view to increasing our tourist industry. Would it be possible for the minister's department to make arrangements with the film industry so that our films could be shown in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We have been doing that during the past few months and have had spectacular results. A great number of shorts have been made in Canada about Canada and circulated to every movie house in the United States. Records descriptive of Canada have been circulated' through all the radio stations in the United States, and I am told by those who have visited there that they are being frequently used. An active promotion program is being carried on under the auspices of the moving-picture industry. I am told that, as a result of the present campaign, two full-length movies will be made in Ontario during the current year.

Some few years ago
several writers visited Ontario, as a result of which a great deal of publicity was obtained. I recall an article by Rex Beach in the Saturday Evening Post. I was wondering if the department had any such plan under consideration. Then I was wondering what plans the department has to further this industry by way of lecturers and speakers in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: This month, in co-operation with the province of Ontario, we are entertaining a group of writers in Ottawa. We have circulated the titles of -books which we think would be appropriate for movies based on Canada. It was a considerable list of most attractive titles. I do not know the value of lectures because I never attend them myself, but perhaps some people do. We have no plans for lecturers.
Sometimes we have them here.

I understand that last year the director of the travel bureau made some
thirty-five appearances on the other side, speaking to service clubs and other organizations. I think the senior officials of the department, including the director of the travel bureau, could serve a most useful purpose by speaking to service clubs and other organizations on the other side. It should be done on a planned basis, so that a great area could be covered. Other efforts like sportsmen's shows and exhibits could be co-ordinated. I really think the amount allocated for the promotion of the tourist industry is small compared with what could really be developed if it were carried on in an aggressive manner.

I have never been able to understand the program and policies of the travel bureau. I appreciate the great work they are doing, but I am of the opinion that there is considerable overlapping in some cases, as I shall explain later, and a conspiracy of silence in other cases.
Some years ago I took up the question of tourist publicity for the district which I have the honour to represent, with a prominent official of the Canadian Pacific. I said to him, "You do not advertise the Okanagan lake; you do not advertise your steamer service; you do not advertise your other services". He admitted it, and then he said, "I'll tell you the reason why. We like to keep people moving along the main line from one big hotel to another. If we advertise your little steamship services it would divert people going from Banff to the coast."
It would almost appear that the dominion government advertising is coincidental with Canadian Pacific advertising. These smaller places with smaller hotels and tourist camps offer excellent facilities for large numbers of people who would be willing to go to the less known places. I can hardly believe that this is accidental. It seems to me that the advertising of the dominion government travel bureau and that of the Canadian Pacific indicates a common policy to advertise in such a way that the large hotels will be filled up and people kept on the main lines of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. Hundreds of these smaller and more attractive hotels and tourist resorts are being overlooked. I should like to know upon what basis the travel bureau advertises, in the United States, tourist facilities in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The federal government can do only a national job. It invites people to come to Canada; not to any part of Canada, but just to come to Canada. It may show the attractions of various parts of Canada,
510G
Supply-Trade and Commerce

but it does not say, "Come to Georgian Bay," or "Come to Quebec City" It does not say, "Come to the Canadian Pacific Hotel at Banff". It says, "Come to Canada". There are other agencies here which do that type of work, the provinces and the transportation companies. They advertise particular resorts and travel between particular points.
I think my hon. friend will appreciate that that is not a job for the dominion government. We simply advertise Canada as a whole. I suggest that the province of British Columbia would be the logical agency to advertise the beauties of Okanagan lake which I enjoyed immensely on my recent visit, even though my purpose in going there was not accomplished.

The minister has said that the job of the travel bureau is a national job. When the director receives an inquiry from someone in the United States, does he write that person and ask if there is any particular section he would like to come to?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes. If a person indicates an interest in a certain, section, full information about that section is given, either by means of dominion government literature or by means of provincial government literature. The province would be advised that such and such a tourist was interested in such and such a resort. There is a complete exchange of information. The proper agency would reply and give the information. We simply do a national job which is intended to be in the interests of every part of Canada.

The minister says the province would be notified that a person wanted to go there, and in turn they would write to that person. Do you also take it up with any local agency, with a chamber of commerce or board of trade? I come from the Kawartha lake section. Would you take it up with the chamber of commerce at Peterborough or the director of tourist publicity?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We notify the province and the province would notify the particular city. The local situation is a provincial responsibility. It might interest my hon. friend to know that the bureau ships out two tons of mail daily, bandies from three thousand to six thousand inquiries daily and has serviced 147,391 inquiries from January to May, 1948.

After looking at some of the exhibits put on by the dominion government-I mentioned this to the director- I believe it would add colour if the Department of Justice would allow one or two mounties with their red coats to accompany the exhibit to the United States. There is no

doubt about it, they are dull. They try to put on a good show, but I believe if they had a mountie on the job all the time it would help. Years ago they used to have mounties. Away back in 1900 or 1901 the Trent waterway development association was able to induce the dominion government to help them put on an exhibit in Grand Central Palace in New York city. We managed to get mounties to go with that. That exhibit was put on for about five years. I would like the minister to comment on the sending of mounties along with exhibits to the United States.
Mention was made of insufficient hotel accommodation, and that complaint is perfectly justified. Some of these hotels are not really fit for tourists to go into. That is why the Ontario government is now, last year and this, having all these tourist resorts, cabins and restaurants inspected to see that they are kept clean. If they are not, the owners are told to clean them up, and if they do not, their licence is cancelled.
Has the director received any complaints from fish and game associations in regard to people going up to James bay and shooting ducks and geese from planes? United States tourists have complained to me about that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The complaints ordinarily go to the fish and game departments of the provinces. We have had complaints, and the air regulations people have taken action.
They have taken action recently?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
What about the mounties?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That is a matter for the Department of Justice. That staff is recruited for the protection of 'Canada, and during the war it was not possible to divert members of the staff. Perhaps now it will be possible again. I will draw the views of the committee to the attention of the Minister of Justice.
I think the director will agree that it is certainly something that should be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is certainly a great advertisement for Canada.

The minister said that the 25 per cent tax was not paid by people from the United States on goods they sent home, but they have all the nuisance of going through customs, and a great many visitors do not know that they can get these goods tax-free for shipment home. I suggest to the minister that it might be wise to go through the list of articles to which the 25

Supply-Trade and Commerce
per cent tax applies with a view to eliminating the tax. I think the results would be more worthwhile to Canada than anything brought in by the tax.

The word "co-ordinate" nearly always frightens me. It nearly always means someone who is put on to help other people work together who probably would work better without a co-ordinator. I am not saying that is true here, because the minister has given us evidence that some real co-ordination is going on. Nevertheless do not let us fool ourselves. As soon as you set up a little kingdom, the king of that kingdom has one great desire in mind, to extend it. He would have to be superhuman if he had not that desire. Therefore I would like to ask a little more about this co-ordination. This has become something quite beyond co-ordination. In the first place, it is spending a lot of money itself. In the second place, it is evidently inviting large numbers of inquiries to be directed to itself. That is not co-ordination. That is setting up a little kingdom of its own. I am not saying that can be avoided. I am only putting it to the minister. It seems to me unfortunate that the inquiries should come in here, then, I presume, be allocated to the provinces, and then be re-allocated to them. I am not wanting to crab this thing because by and large I think a good job is being done, but does the minister not think there is a real danger of allowing this branch to grow up and up and having inquiries directed to itself? Do those inquiries need 'to come here? Should they not in the first instance be directed to where they are to be acted on?
Another thing; on'e of the finest ways of wasting money, if one does not watch it, is to give a lot of money to an advertising agency to spend. They will spend it-leave that to them. But whether that advertising produces results commensurate with the expenditure is a question. My query is whether that kind of advertising is anything like as good as money spent on personal contacts.
The minister spoke about publications brought out by the department-"Skiing in Canada", "Rod and Reel". It seems to me that these are a natural thing for a central body to handle, because they deal with conditions across the country. But I would like to hear the minister say a word more on coordination, which frightens me so much. Mr. Dolan is a sensible man, so far as I know, who would be able to get people to work together. The minister spoke of having meetings with the provinces. I would like to know whether he is satisfied that this co-ordination is real co-ordination and is not creating a new
department here which is doing a lot of work that is just a duplication of what ought to be done in the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I have been associated with this bureau for quite a few years; it used to be in the Department of Transport. Care is taken that there is no overlapping. Our interprovincial relations are exceedingly good in this matter. This is one field of endeavour where the provinces work very closely with the dominion. Through co-ordination a lot of duplicate work is avoided. Certain work is allotted to the federal field, other work to the provinces, and still other work to the railways and bus companies, which are also large advertisers in other countries. All this advertising is co-ordinated. You will seldom pick up a magazine and see an obvious duplication of advertising from Canada, which I think is a tribute to the work of the federal bureau. By and large it is doing a good job, and a better job each year, in avoiding duplication in the field of advertising.
My hon. friend asks whether I think advertising is good. I have not the faintest idea. Some people ask if movie publicity is good. I do not know. But most great enterprises do a great deal of advertising and must think it is good. I would think the advertising we do in United States publications is about the right kind of advertising, judging by the standards of other great enterprises.
What about having a large number of inquiries directed here which have to be re-routed to the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is not a matter of directing them here. The advertising put out by the bureau carries the stamp of the federal bureau; the advertising put out by the provinces carries the stamp of the provinces; the advertising put out by the railroads carries the stamp of the railroads. The bureau is a clearing house. If people inquire of the federal government about fishing in Nova Scotia we would not want to say: We know nothing about it. The bureau acts as a universal clearing house to get the inquiries into the right channels.
Would it mar the appearance of the advertisements if they showed the various provincial offices to which inquiries could be directed?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I think that would hardly be feasible. I think you must have a clearing house, and the present system I think works fairly well.

I think it is pretty well agreed that we should have more and better tourist
Supply-Trade and Commerce

accommodation. I have been approached by possibly a hundred good clean-cut returned boys who want to go into the tourist business and build cottages of some description to take care of visitors to Canada. The difficulty is they have no funds. They do not want the money given to them particularly, but they want to borrow it. Has the department ever given any consideration to setting up some sort of trust fund or mortgage board of some description through which assistance might be given these boys who have a desire to go into that business in Canada? If that were done we might build up something which might be worthwhile.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: A good deal of thought has been given to it. The director of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation developed quite a plan, and it is being studied now by the Bank of Canada and by the government. I do not say that it will be put into force next year. It probably requires more working over. It is a fairly comprehensive plan of financing tourist establishments in selected areas. It is quite a big plan. As my hon. friend will appreciate, it takes a good deal of money. It is not a thing to be jumped into immediately, but it is certainly worthy of the consideration it is receiving.
It is receiving consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.

Some of us may have wondered why, after all the portfolios he has occupied, the minister was selected to be Minister of Trade and Commerce. This afternoon I think we know why, because he has shown that he is the most versatile man in the government. He has answered questions about financing of soldiers, the mounted police, and so on.
In examining this item, I find there is one thing we have overlooked. I do not know whether the government is overlooking it, but in our discussions I believe we have overlooked assistance toward bringing tourist business to Canada. The tourist business in Canada is tremendous. I think the department, and I know the various governmental services in the provinces, are bidding for the tourist traffic. A very good job is being done in that regard. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Leeds that we are just about taxed to our capacity as far as accommodation is concerned. We have various travel associations. I have been associated with the Blue Water Highway Association and the Huronic Historic Sites Association, which embraces that area from Orillia to Barrie, Midland and Owen Sound, which is considered to be the one place where civilization in this country began.

I want to put on the record a few figures which I thought would be of interest to the committee with regard to what tourist travel really means. I am going to refer to the Col-lingwood area. I could select the city of Owen Sound, the scenic city of Canada, where the atmosphere is so invigorating and the scenery so beautiful; but for fear of being accused of boosting my own home town and constituency, I shall take the neighbouring town, Colling-wood. The report I have is for the year 1946, when we had a survey made at Wasaga beach. It is not as up to date as I should like to have it. We have not the figures for 1947. Wasaga beach has a population of around 300 persons, I would say. In eight weeks in 1946 they had a daily average of 55,000 persons. Twenty-five per cent were citizens of the United States. Therefore seventy-five per cent of our own people were patronizing that beach.
We have been seeking to encourage our farmers to believe that the tourist business means as much to them as it does to the businessman. We have encouraged them to invest their funds in tourist associations and to assist in promoting the tourist trade. I shall now give figures to show the amount of food that was consumed and produced on farms adjacent to Wasaga beach in 1946: poultry, 434,840 pounds; butter, 68,000 pounds; eggs, 536,925 dozen; meat, 2,202,000 pounds; vegetables, raw, 4,800,000 pounds; and milk, 186,000 gallons.
In a discussion of the tourist business we hear a lot about United States tourists. We are certainly glad to have the United States tourists; probably we are happier now than ever before because of our exchange situation. It means a great deal to have this tremendous export business, .so to speak, of the goods consumed in our own country. I leave that thought with the minister. I am mot suggesting for one moment that the government have not had that thought in mind, but the development of our interprovincial and inter-community tourist travel is very important. Generally speaking, however, when we compare the United States tourists who come to Canada, with the vast numbers of our own people who spend their winters in the south in the more moderate climate, I do not know how much we are ahead of the game in the year; but I do know that, in the matter of putting money into circulation, the encouragement of travel gives opportunities and advantages to see our own country, which, after all, so few Canadians know. It affords opportunity for travel in Canada, and that is the one trait we should seek to develop, because we have much in common. Let us have as much of the other traffic from outside our country as we can attract, but let us seek to provide suitable

Supply-Trade and Commerce
accommodation for those who are visiting us, so that they will go away with some appreciation of the holiday they have had.
We have certainly a lack of modern accommodation. The province of Ontario is now giving consideration to the inspection of tourist homes, which is all to the good. I am one of those who would like to congratulate and compliment Mr. Leo Dolan. I have had many long years of association with him indirectly, and I appreciate very much the work he is doing. I am glad to see this sum in the estimates, and I hope it will be well spent for the general benefit of the tourist traffic in Canada.

I should just like to say this on the question I asked on this item. The figures I asked for are not contained in the annual report of the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is pertinent, because what I am trying to find is the behaviour pattern of the United States tourist when he comes to Canada. It has been said generally that the United States tourist comes to Canada and buys a hot dog and that the Canadian, tourist goes to the United States and wants a cabana at S40 a day, or he spends six weeks in a de luxe hotel in Florida. What I should like to find out is this. How many United States tourists come to Canada? What do they spend? How many spend three days or a week in Canada? What do they do particularly when they are here? In other words, what I should like to have is a breakdown of the value of the tourist trade to us in Canada.
I have heard it said that the tourist trade is worth $300 million to Canada in a year. I have also heard that that is an over-estimate. We should have an analysis of the tourist trade so that we can encourage it where it is most valuable. I make one suggestion. The hon. member for Calgary West has made this suggestion before. I refer to the Banff and Jasper national parks, and particularly to the development of those parks in the winter. There are three million people in the United States who ski. According to the best information I can get, the average expenditure is at least $100. There is a traffic of $300 million in skiing alone. Something should be done in the national parks, lake Louise, and Banff, so that we would end up by having these great hotels open in the winter as well as in the summer. There is a tremendous field out there. I should like to have some idea of how many United States tourists come in for two days or three days, and where they go and what their expenditures are. I mention again the development of the Rockies in the winter, because the skiing season is just double the summer season. The people who come to
visit us in the winter are not the 24-hour tourists; they are people who come and spend a week or two weeks. On the whole they are much more valuable to us. I wonder whether the department has a breakdown of these figures or whether they can be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am advised that a study of that kind is published each year by the bureau of statistics, showing the effect of the tourist traffic on the international balance of payments. I have asked the director to send a copy to my hon. friend today, so that he can have the latest information.
There is no study of the behaviour pattern of the tourist when he gets here?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes; it covers that.
That would be most valuable. It would show the type of tourist coming in, the type who spends a week or a couple of weeks.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I will send a copy to my hon. friend.

I join with others who have commended the minister for the expansion of the department, and also in their expressions of appreciation of the headway made by the tourist bureau. Federal concern in this whole subject originated with Senator Dennis of Nova Scotia, who brought the matter before the senate, where a committee was set up of which he was chairman, and a policy was enunciated. The tourist bureau has developed from these beginnings into the present Dominion Government Travel Bureau, which is its present full name.
Reference has been made to other parts of Canada, but in this discussion I have not heard anyone refer to the maritime provinces, and that is a serious neglect, in view of the fact that the present tourist bureau in Canada had its origin in Nova Scotia with Senator Dennis, and the director, Mr. Dolan, is also from Nova Scotia; yet the maritime provinces have not been mentioned.
I do not believe there is a section of Canada that has greater attractions for the tourist than our provinces by the sea. Every part of the maritimes has its particular attractions. The visitor will find a great deal of enjoyment, health and hospitality in the Annapolis valley, the south shore, unequalled scenic beauty of Cape Breton island-I do not think it can be equalled on the continent of North America-along the Northumberland straits, in the county of Cumberland, and Prince Edward Island with our warm sea water and clear invigorating air. We hear of
Supply-Trade and Commerce

millions, indeed tens of millions of dollars being spent in the development of tourist resorts in the state of Maine, but there is no such expenditure in the maritime provinces where we have equal or greater attractions.
The minister should make a special effort to induce more people from central Canada to visit the maritimes, thus saving Canadian dollars. Large numbers go there now, and once they familiarize themselves with the attractions and the healthful surroundings, many decide to establish summer homes there. For every one that goes there now, there should be hundreds. No part of the tourist business holds out greater possibilities for development than the maritimes

Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
I commend the minister for the development of this branch. I know how busy the director is at this season. I picked up my home paper today before coming into the chamber, and I see that a special invitation has been extended to Mr. Dolan to address the board of trade of Amherst, but he replied that he was unable to do so because he was too busy serving the people in central Canada. He could not give special attention to our part of Canada. Perhaps I am not quoting him correctly, but I think that is, in effect, his reply. At any rate, I am pleased to support this appropriation.
I support the request made by my hon. friend (Mr. Adamson) for a breakdown of the amount involved in the tourist industry, and I would ask the minister to separate it into provinces and seasons.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am not sure what the breakdown is; I have not seen it. Such as it is, however, I will have it sent to you.

Another suggestion I have to make, and I offer it in the belief that it will produce good results, is that when the next session opens iwe should set up a House of Commons committee on the tourist industry. I know a committee of this kind has been functioning elsewhere, but I am confident that a committee of the House of Commons, representative of all the provinces, would make a great contribution to the promotion of the tourist industry.
If the tourist industry is worth $300 million a year, it is one of the first two or three industries in Canada, and an analysis should be made showing how the money comes in.

I, too, am pleased to join with the hon. member for Cumberland and others in support of this vote. There are two things

I would say. First I wish to compliment the director on his activities. His work is excellent, and that is to be expected; he is a mari-timer, full of energy. He is one of those whom we had to export to promote national affairs. An hon. member suggested that the director might be made a deputy minister. I do not think that is really intended; but in this department, as in all departments of government, the work of those who direct matters in the field is to a large extent restricted by red tape. There are many things that could and should be done quickly; but it is necessary for the field workers, who have the actual job of administration, to go back to the deputy minister and finally to the minister, and by the time certain orders and regulations that are called for have been got through to the minister, the tourist season is over.
I would suggest that the person who directs the tourist bureau should be given considerable latitude and authority to carry out the work, without the necessity of going back and checking and rechecking and getting orders, and all that kind of thing.
There is one point I would make in regard to promoting the tourist industry of the maritime provinces, and that is with particular reference to my own end of the country, Cape Breton island. The tourists who come to that part of the country are not in the ordinary category of tourists. They axe largely people who migrated from that part of the country to the United States and particularly to the New England states. There are thousands of them, and these people would like to come back, but one thing that militates against a larger number returning to that part of the country is the condition of the secondary roads leading into certain sections. Did it ever occur to the minister to inaugurate a direct plane service from that airport in Sydney to Boston or other airports in the New England states?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We have that now.
A direct flight from Sydney?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It stops at Halifax.
Yes, on a roundabout course. It costs a great deal more money. That is something like getting from Ottawa-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It does not cost more money.

Yes, it goes to Halifax and Moncton; and you have to roam all over the country and pay a great deal more money in order to get to that destination. I am suggesting a direct flight which would cut the time down considerably as well as the expense. Thousands more people would be

Supply-Trade and Commerce
brought in if that kind of service were established in place of what we have at the present time.
The tourist industry in Nova Scotia is one of our major ones today. Just recently I saw a report by the minister of industry of Nova Scotia, and the amount of money left by United States tourists in Nova Scotia staggered me. I never thought it ran into the figures shown in the report. If that report is true for that section of the country, I think it is true for nearly all of Canada. This would be one of the greatest industries assisting in the cutting down of our shortage of United States dollars, if we could bring more people in and have them spend their money here. I merely rose to make the suggestion of a direct plane service between that Sydney station and eastern United States stations, because I think it would pay for itself.
In the second place, I wanted to say that I appreciated the work done by the director. I have had considerable contact with him. He is active and always on the job. The field workers in all departments such as this one should have a great deal more authority than they have. If the line of red tape back through government, which is necessary under the present arrangements, were cut considerably and if a little more authority were given to these workers, I believe they could do a better job in promoting the industry.

I wish to solicit the support of the minister to the end that he may use his influence with his colleagues in the other departments. I have reference to the final road leading to our national park, which is our drawing card for tourists in Prince Edward Island. A short distance of road- about three-quarters of a mile-in the park area is under dispute. The dominion government do not wish to take it over; yet they claim they own it. The provincial government will not repair it. Between the two of them, the road has really become a mud-hole for about a mile over which tourists must travel in order to get down to the beach and also to get to the finest golf links, they say, in Canada.
One other thing we have appreciated in the advertising in the last couple of years is the fact that Prince Edward Island is now on most of the maps I have seen. Prior to two years ago, we were put on about once in every ten years.
The hon. member advertises the province every day in the house.

However, this improvement is probably due to the fact that advertising
experts have found that there is in Prince Edward Island a tourist resort equal to any. Now we are getting a better return from the advertising. As I mentioned before, until last year we could not get proper accommodation for most of the tourists who came there. But this year I think we shall be able to take care of twice as many tourists as we have taken care of in any other season. We are proud to say that, through good advertising and through having a good place to which to come, I understand that the Governor General of Canada is to vacation in our province this summer. We hope that this will be one of the finest advertisements we have ever had for the tourist business in Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I may say that I have a special interest in that bit of road. In my house I have a handsome piece of plate awarded to the victor of the tournament held at the opening of that golf course, and I will ask my colleagues to give consideration to this matter.
I merely rise, Mr. Chairman, so that the public will know that there is someone from Alberta here.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If this item could be considered carried, I should be glad. It is necessary for me to leave now in order to catch a plane, and I shall turn over the responsibility to my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 245. Departmental administration, $623,428.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have some remarks to make on this item, Mr. Chairman; but at the outset I should like you to give some indication to the committee, for its guidance, as to the extent to which members may discuss, under this section, the subject matter of additional grants to assist the construction of hospitals, and other health matters proposed by the Prime Minister in his statement in the house about a month ago. The Prime Minister at that time indicated that supplementary appropriations would be introduced in due course to deal with that matter. I think it would be of assistance to all the members of the committee, Mr. Chairman, if you would indicate at the outset if that matter may be discussed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
No. I would have to say immediately that it would not be in order to discuss it under this item.

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakeroldname: Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I say one word in that connection. I had a chance of informally discussing this matter with several members of the house, including the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. I suggested that, as there would naturally be great interest in the details of the program announced by the Prime Minister, and that, as the supplementary estimates in connection with that program are not yet before the house, we might avoid duplication of discussion if we confined the general discussion in connection with this department to the moment when we have before us the supplementary estimates, which would give ample opportunity for a wider discussion and thereby possibly avoid discussing the same matter twice. I am in the hands of the committee in the matter, but I understood from the conversation I had with other hon. members that such procedure would likely be in accord with their views and wishes in the matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
May I just say that if a ruling is made to that effect, which will be binding on the committee, it will, I am sure, be entirely satisfactory to all of us. We all wish to be graded by the same ruling in this matter. It is of the highest importance. If you make that ruling, Mr. Chairman, we will adhere loyally to it. We understand, however, that when the supplementary appropriations are brought down, they will be brought down at a time that will afford an ample opportunity lor discussion of this matter.
In other years it will be recalled that in the discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare much has been said about the kind of program members have felt should be brought in. If we leave over that kind of discussion for the supplementary appropriations, then I suggest it is most important that the government allow ample opportunity for it, and that it should bring in the supplementary appropriations at a time which will give hon. members ample opportunity for discussion. I suggest that we should not be caught at the last moment in a rush which may lead to glossing over a matter of such great importance. Would you give a ruling, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I shall have to rule that it would not be in order to discuss matters which will be brought in later with the supplementary estimates. We shall have to confine our remarks to the item now under discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. There are some remarks of a general nature I
[The Deputy Chairman.]
should like to make respecting the estimates of this department.
We have before us increased estimates for the fiscal year. The estimates for the new fiscal year amount to $345,660,705, whereas those of the previous year were $319,990,101, showing that the department is budgeting this year for an increased expenditure of $25,670,604. This department is now the second greatest spending department among all the departments of government, its expenditures being exceeded only by the Department of Finance, and in that instance only because of the charges paid annually through that department on the national debt.
For those who like to compare expenditures on these vitally important subjects of health and welfare with expenditures on other matters of essential importance, I mention in passing that the expenditures this year for the Department of National Defence are $232,408,239.95, and that the expenditures this year for the Department of National Health and Welfare will therefore exceed those of the Department of National Defence by about $113 million. When the supplementary estimates are introduced, as forecast by the Prime Minister some weeks ago, we may expect further substantially increased expenditures in this department, marking it as the department through which there is the greatest expenditure of funds for services in the Dominion of Canada.
These figures demonstrate the importance of the department and the importance of the task upon which the committee is now engaged in reviewing the estimates. I make no apology for alluding at this point to a matter to which I have referred in previous sessions because, unhappily, this is about the only opportunity one has of adverting to it.
I have had on the order paper for the last four sessions the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, standing order G3 be amended by adding after subsection 1: (m) on public health, welfare, social security and housing to consist of thirty-five members, ten of whom shall constitute a quorum.
This proposal is for the establishment of a standing committee on health, welfare, social security and housing. We have a great many committees of the house, some of which function actively, and some of which do not. But we have not yet, even in this year of 1948, established a committee charged with the responsibility of reviewing matters of the kind to which I have referred. I believe most members, when confronted with those matters, would frankly concede them to be of the highest importance. Great advantages would accrue to the house from the appoint-

Supply-Health and Welfare
ment of a standing committee on health, welfare, social security and housing. The value of such a committee would be demonstrated not alone in the matter of reviewing estimates, although at a time like this I suggest its value would be clearly demonstrated. I am thinking more of the duty placed upon hon. members to inform themselves of all aspects of these important matters.
We gather information from reports-which often are stale by the time they reach us. We try to keep ourselves informed through the press and other publications. Hon. members, however, have not an opportunity of questioning officials of the department at first hand, a procedure which I conceive to be one which would bring great benefit to the House of Commons by way of obtaining additional information and making the house better informed as to the functions of the department. Such a committee would assist the house greatly in determining where money can wisely be spent for purposes of health and welfare, or where it might be more wisely spent than it is at the present time. It would give an opportunity, furthermore, for the proper analysis of proposals submitted by various interested organizations such as medical and welfare groups, those who are making a study of housing problems, and labour organizations which have done much in giving assistance and oftentimes a lead in the approach to social problems.
A committee of the house could go into matters of that kind in a really useful and efficient manner, at first hand. Present procedure denies us that opportunity. We can put our questions to the minister. He will answer certain questions; but we do not have firsthand contact with the information in the minds of the officials.
I believe the minister has sympathy for this proposal. I would urge upon him to press it, and to the limit of his resources to endeavour to bring about an amendment of the rules of the house which would permit the appointment of such a committee. It seems to me utterly useless for a private member to place on the order paper a resolution in which he seeks to amend the rules, even where those rules appear to be archaic. As I have pointed out, my resolution has been on the order paper for four sessions; and at the rate we are going I suppose it will be there for fifty years before it will ever be reached. But the government has it in its power to advance proposals of the kind, if it wishes to take the subject in hand. I urge upon the minister that he regard this not only as an opportunity, but as a duty.
When we come to a review of the estimates we see at once the usefulness of such a committee. I do not wish to thresh old straw, because I have spoken on this subject before.
I must say, however, that I believe the house approaches its task of reviewing estimates inadequately equipped for the purpose. That inadequate equipment is not the fault of members of the house, nor do I think it is altogether the fault of the government. I do say wre must revise our procedure with a view to improving its efficiency. No business organization in the country would approach the problem of budgeting for its fiscal needs in the ensuing year without knowing precisely what was expended in the previous one.
In the present instance we are dealing with the expenditure of about a third of a billion dollars, but we have not before us the expenditures made by the department last year. We have to assist us in our comparisons only the appropriations which were voted last year. We do not know in the case of any item to what extent the appropriation is exhausted. We do not know to what extent the appropriation proved to be more than was required. The committee is simply working at least in the dusk, if not in the dark, in proceeding with its budgetary task on that basis. What the committee ought to have before it, before it ever settles down to this task, is the full detail of last year's expenditures under these items.
So that I may put myself on a common footing with the minister, at this point I am going to ask him to give to the committee when he speaks-this will save the time of the committee of the whole-details of the expenditures made last year in connection with every item appearing on pages 33 and 34 of the estimates. I asked that last year, but the minister chose not to give it and I was com' pelled to ask for the previous year's expenditure on each item as it was reached. In order to save time, I hope that this year the minister will give the committee a statement in advance showing the actual expenditure under each item. I know that will save time, because I for one intend to make it my business to find out the actual expenditure last year on each item. In the external affairs committee where we were reviewing the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, we were furnished, before we began our task, with detailed expenditures under each item of the estimates. That was of great assistance to the committee and saved much time.
There are some other matters of a specific nature which I intend to take up, but at this stage I ask, as the first item, that the minister furnish us with further information. One reason
Supply-Health and Welfare

why it is necessary to ask for this information is that the reports we have before us are stale by the time they reach us. Of course, that situatioh is not peculiar to this department; it is inherent under the procedure under which we work. The last report we have is for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1947. The information in that report is now fifteen months old. Conditions change and a report of that kind is of limited use at this stage. I ask the minister to supply us with certain general information. First, will he tell the committee the number of employees in the department at the present date. According to the annual report to which I have referred, the number of employees in the department at March 31, 1947, was:
Permanent	 303
Temporary	 1,625
Total	 1,928
I am sure the committee will be impressed with the small proportion of employees on a permanent footing and the high proportion of employees on a temporary footing. We appreciate that this is a young department, having been in existence now for a trifle under four years, but one would expect that by this time a greater number of employees would be on a permanent footing. I think it will interest the committee to know the number of employees today and to have that number broken down as between permanent and temporary employees. I have already asked the minister to furnish us with the detailed expenditures of last year.
There is another matter which I am sure will interest the committee, because the committee has shown its interest in it in previous sessions. There are many amounts scattered through the various branches of this department under the euphonious title, "Educational and informational publicity." I note that the amounts budgeted for this year aggregate $406,850, whereas last year the amount budgeted for was $480,507. It would appear that there has been a reduction of $73,657 in these items for so-called educational and informational publicity, formerly called "publicity and information." However. I have a suspicion that if we compare the actual expenditures last year with the amounts estimated for the present year we shall find that it is not a decrease but an increase that is being estimated for now. I ask the minister to give the total expenditures last year under these items of educational and informational publicity.
I am also interested in the items of travelling expenses. There are many of them scattered through the various items, I think approximately thirty. According to my calculation,

these amounts total no less than $643,000. Last year the aggregate amount budgeted for was $515,650. The estimates this year show an increase of exactly 25 per cent over those of last year. The committee will wish to know why there should be such a substantial increase in the travelling expenses for this year. In case any wrong inference should be drawn, I ask hon. members to look at page 190 of the estimates. They will then see that the amounts provided under travelling expenses apparently have no relationship to the expenses of delegates to international conferences. We know that leading officials of the department on both health and welfare sides are being asked to attend international conferences at 'New York and elsewhere, and under the departmental administration item there is an item on page 190, reading as follows:
Allowances and other expenses of delegates to international conferences, $10,000.
From that, I assume that the other items of travelling expenses have no relationship to the expenses of delegates attending international conferences. I again observe that the travelling expenses for this year show an increase of 25 per cent over the estimates of last year. I think the committee will wish to know the actual amount expended last year on travelling expenses because, if the estimates of this department run true to form and history repeats itself, I believe it will be found that the amount actually expended last year was less than the amount estimated, and therefore the increase in the estimates of this year over the expenditures of last year will be more than 25 per cent.
For the purpose of saving time, I ask the minister at this stage to put on the record the information that he has in relation to family allowances. The kind of information I refer to is to be found on pages 4465, 4466 and 4467 of Hansard of last year. If that information were put on the record at this stage it would give hon. members an opportunity to prepare their questions on the matter, and time would be saved. If it is left until the item is reached before the information is put on the record, more questions will probably have to be asked because we would not have the figures before us. I make that suggestion in the interests of saving time.
I turn now to another subject. I shall be brief, because I do not desire to prolong these remarks as I believe the committee will wish to discuss the items. The subject I should like to mention now is the dominion-provincial relations with respect to health and welfare. I have no intention of trespassing on a subject which will be discussed when the supplementary estimates are before us. But we do

olio
Supply-Health and Welfare
know that a conference was held in Ottawa this week, attended by officials of all the provincial departments of health, at the invitation of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. If the minister is in a position to give a report on that conference, without revealing matters which should not yet properly be revealed, I would urge him ito do so. The country and, I am sure, this house are anxious to know the subjects that were discussed at that conference, what success attended its deliberations, and what action may be expected to ensue from the conference.
It is significant, I think, Mr. Chairman, that when an invitation was issued by the dominion authorities for the holding of a dominion-provincial conference in this field, which requires joint dominion and provincial action if it is to be properly covered, all the provinces readily responded. I think that indicates to all and sundry the readiness of the governments of all the provinces to meet together with the dominion and with their sister provinces to discuss matters pertaining to health and welfare for the general advantage of all Canadians. I hope that that start will be followed up and that the dominion government will follow through now by calling another dominion-provincial conference or conferences with a view to bringing about common consultation and common action in matters of common concern to the dominion and the provinces.
We see great needs to be met in the field of health and welfare in Canada. Many of the needs are of critical proportions. I know the house is familiar with them. On the health side we have a critical shortage of nurses, a critical shortage of hospital accommodation, and a serious shortage of doctors, particularly in certain areas. We see certain diseases increasing in their incidence in Canada. For instance, I am sure the house was impressed by the report issued last fall by the Canadian Tuberculosis Association, calling attention to the necessity of an intensified tuberculosis program across the dominion, and pointing out that ground was lost in the previous year in Canada in the fight against this scourge. A total of 5,797 Canadians died of tuberculosis in 1946. The death rate from tuberculosis climbed from 45-9 per 100,000 of population in 1945, the all-time low, to 47-2 per 100,000 in 1946. Perhaps the minister will have further figures for the full year 1947. Perhaps those figures are not yet available. But let no one think the fight against tuberculosis has been won when we see this scourge raising its ugly head once again in this manner.
Mental disease in Canada appears to be on the increase. Last year more than 53,000 5849-324J
persons were treated for mental disease in institutions for that purpose in Canada, and the cost this year of fighting mental disease in Canada will approximate $30,000,000. That is only one aspect of the tremendous cost of disease and does not take into account all the impairment of health, the impairment of efficiency, and the loss of production of wealth in Canada by reason of illness and impairment of faculties.
The committee will wish to hear from the minister what precisely has been expended from dominion revenues on research. We hear a great deal of talk about research, but there has been altogether too much inclination to leave the burden of meeting the cost of research on the provinces and on institutions such as universities and hospitals which are largely supported by provincial and, in some cases, by municipal revenues. The committee will wish to hear from the minister exactly what sums out of dominion revenues were actually devoted to research in the field of health in Canada last year. The impression I think of most Canadians who have studied this problem is that research has largely been starved in Canada.
Again, on the welfare side, we find similar needs and similar shortages. There will be opportunity as the debate proceeds to discuss some of the needs. I mention, in passing, the serious shortage of trained social workers in Canada. I am glad to see that grants are proposed again this year to assist schools of social work in Canada. They are needing assistance because they will need to turn out more and more young people trained for social work if we are to have any hope at all of meeting the needs in this field, We cannot hope to hold our social welfare workers in Canada in places where they are so badly needed at the present time unless their salaries are commensurate with the need and importance of their work. We have been losing, over a period of years, many of our best trained social workers to the United States and in other avenues of employment, because of the inadequacy of the remuneration offered to them in welfare organizations and in public service at various levels of government.
My concluding observation in this preliminary debate is this. In the vitally important fields of national health and national welfare there can be no standing still. New needs are pressing upon us all the time as life becomes more complicated on the social side. On the health side the tremendous loss that ill health and disease take in toll each year has made such an impression on the Canadian people that I believe they are fully convinced that

the health of all the people of Canada is the concern of all the people of Canada. I am glad that there will be an opportunity later, on the supplementary appropriations to develop our views on this point further. I leave this thought before the committee. Whatever promises to assist in meeting our problems with respect to national health will, I am sure, be readily subscribed to by all parts of the house.

That, of course, is one of the features of the work of this department which, at the moment, attracts great interest because it is new, and because it is a beginning which we hope will develop into something really worthwhile in the not too distant future.
However, as we go through these estimates which are before us today, I note that there is again the usual item covering health insurance studies. I hope that when we reach that item the minister will have something to say about it. I remind him that last year we were disappointed over here-the disappointment was expressed in particular by my colleague, the hon. member for Mackenzie-to discover that all the money voted the previous year for this purpose had not been expended. In fact we felt that not sufficient work was being done in this field. I note now that there is a decrease in the amount asked for under health insurance studies this year. I am sorry to note that. It seems to me that the opposite ought to be the case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If the hon. member will wait until the item is called I can explain it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

All I am saying is that I am warning the minister that this is an item iu which we are particularly interested.
Another item which we shall have something to say about relates to the question of family allowances, and I should like to ask

the minister to be ready in particular to tell us whether consideration has been given to the request made to him a number of times regarding children of immigrants coming to this country. That is a point which the hon. member for Dauphin made most recently the other evening. We feel that it is unfair to children who come to this country to be put to the disadvantage of being denied the benefit of family allowances until they have been here for three years.
When the family allowances legislation was brought in it was emphasized by the Prime Minister that it was for the children, and that they were not to suffer any disabilities for causes over which they had no control. A case in point is that of illegitimate children. It was pointed out that it was not their fault, and that they should get the benefit of the allowances, as they do, and rightly so. It is hardly a comparable case, but in a sense it is, and I suggest that this is an amendment to the act-if that is the way it has to be done-that is overdue. I hope the minister will have something to say about it when the item is reached. I do not recall whether we had a great deal of discussion about this phase of the matter when the bill was before the house in 1944. The likelihood is that at that time we were not thinking in terms of the more extensive immigration that we are having at the present time.
Another of the items in which we are particularly interested is that relating to blind pensions. I speak of blind persons separately from old age pension recipients to emphasize the fact that the time has come for special legislation for these people. The minister knows of the representations that have been made by the various organizations representing the blind, and I hope that we might get some word from the minister this year as to changes which might be in prospect with reference to legislation affecting the blind.
In particular I should like to urge that the time has come for us to spend a little more money on the prevention of blindness. It seems to be the case-maybe I am overstating it so as ito drive home my point-that a person who is in danger of becoming blind is unable to get financial assistance that might be necessary to procure the medical attention to prevent it. Rather, he is told to go back home and wait until the blindness has overtaken him and then he can qualify for the pension. As I say, Mr. Chairman, maybe I have overstated it a bit, but I have done so to emphasize the point, and I hope that the minister may have something to say along this line that will indicate some new and better legislation with respect to blindness and blind pensions.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Lastly, when we reach the item having to do with old age pensions I hope that we may have some better news from the minister than has yet been forecast during this session. The day that the Prime Minister made his announcement about the health program there were rumours about that announcement around this house of rumours in which we live. The rumour was partly correct, but only partly, because many people around thought the announcement was also going to contain some amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act itself. I hope that the minister will have something to say to us along that line, while we are dealing with his estimates.
I know it is only a year since we amended the Old Age Pensions Act and raised the basic amount to S30 a month. Once an amendment like that has been made, there is always a tendency to sit back and accept it as sufficient for the time being; but I submit to the minister that what has happened to the cost of living-and as chairman of a certain committee he knows all about it-during the year which has passed since the amendment was made, calls for an improvement in the standard of living that we make possible for our old age pensioners. I hope that the minister will not try to pass this back to the provinces again. We can indulge in that kind of political warfare if we want to among the various provinces of this country, but I hope that we shall not do that here in this house. The thing that I deplore is that this question has been made a football, passed back and forth from one level of government to another, with the result that the old age pension varies from province to province, and the old age pensioners themselves are the victims.
I feel strongly that the time has come to increase the amount and to put it on a nationwide basis. There are two or three different approaches to this question which I suggest to the minister. One would be the implementation of the federal government's offer to the provinces back in 1945. I feel that the failure of two provinces to sign dominion-provincial financial agreements is not sufficient excuse for the failure of the government to go ahead with the implementation of these proposals, at least for the people of the provinces that have agreed. But I go further than that. I do not feel that the people in the two central provinces should suffer because their provincial governments have not seen fit to make certain agreements with the federal authorities at Ottawa.

Having regard to national health conditions in Canada, I feel that this house owes more to its members than just this voluntary committee on health that we have. I brought this matter up a year ago. I made an appeal for a committee of this house to examine into certain things. There are two salient facts before this house and we should not lose sight of them. As I have repeated time and time again in this house, you cannot get by the fact that forty-two per cent to forty-four per cent of the young men who were called up for service were found to be unfit. If the percentage of unfitness was so low in that group, there is no doubt that it is much lower in other age groups. From the standpoint of national defence, no nation can be strong with forty-two per cent to forty-four per cent of its young men unfit.
The other fact to which I referred is one which cannot be disputed. We congratulate the minister or any other person concerned that the infant mortality rate is gradually dropping. At the present time it is 5-2 per thousand of live births. But you cannot get away from the fact that the percentage in the United States is 3-8. That nation has a large southern population and large cities with large congested areas. It does not stand to reason that in this country, with twelve million people, we should have a higher infant mortality rate than has the United States. Something is radically wrong. Such matters as cancer, tuberculosis and that sort of thing will naturally come up when the supplementary estimates are discussed, as will also the question of hospital beds and in fact practically all the most important items that come up in the main estimates.

But in order to put a statement on the record, I suppose I should go back to what happened during the war years. There was a time in 1941 and 1942 and again in 1943 when steel was in very short supply, not only here but also in the United States. It was required, as hon. gentlemen know, for all kinds of construction, but particularly for war purposes. It was felt by the government at that time that a contribution of .this sort was little enough for a venture of the kind that was undertaken at Atikokan. The order in council which was passed in 1942 sets out that the development of the mine would be advantageous to Canada and a protection against a possible shortage

of ore to meet war requirements. It is true that the war is over, and to that extent the position has changed; but the position has not changed in so far as the shortage of iron and steel is concerned. Anyone who has to build ships or planes, or to make additions or extensions to industry, knows how difficult it is to get iron and steel. I have in mind several examples at the moment in my own department where the construction of ships is being held up, or the date on which a ship was to have been delivered is delayed because of lack of the required steel. Therefore, as I said a moment ago, the purpose of this in the wrar years was to pool some of our resources. We pooled our shipping; we also pooled this, and from it we got treatment other than we would have received had we not been able to place this in the pool.
