I do not think it is necessary for me to go over the history of the inauguration of the National Harbours Board Act in 1936, and to deal with the development of the board under present conditions. All hon. members are fairly familiar with that. I should like to deal with it as we see it from a local standpoint. What I shall say with respect to the port of Halifax applies equally to practically all the seven ports. I make that statement because I have heard criticisms from each and every port district throughout Canada and from members representing constituencies in which the national harbours board operates under the present system.
I do not think it is possible under that system to give as direct attention and supervision as would be the case if we were operating under local committees; and in my view, from a local standpoint, that supervision is necessary. Someone will say, "Look at the record since 1938. See how our revenues have increased. See how our expenditures have been kept down." But that is not the whole answer in business. Efficiency plays an important part. On the other hand the greater interest brought about by the use of local advisory committees develops just as great efficient, creates a greater interest in the ports and secures business which would otherwise be lost.
I honestly believe that if we had had a local advisory committee last year we would not have lost the freight we did lose through its being diverted to Portland, or other United States ports. The same applies to the amount of business being diverted to those ports at the present time. I feel that there are items which at the present time would help in the development of the port of Halifax which, on account of the attitude taken by the members of the national harbours board, are lost. When I say that, I make no reflection upon the ability of the board-. I am simply stating that they are so far away from local ports that they have not the same interest as would people who are directly connected with them.
Once or twice a year members of the board visit Vancouver at the extreme west, and on other occasions they come east. But their visits are so brief that they cannot possibly get into close touch with matters relating to the development of the port; and I feel this could be done by local authorities.
I do not want the minister to say, "Do you want us to go back to the old system?" It is true that at the present time there is on the order paper a resolution suggesting that we revert to the old system. I am not proposing that this evening; that matter will be dealt with at the proper time. I do say, however, that the minister should now give serious consideration to taking action to bring into effect the recommendations laid down in the Gibb report. That report was made in the best interests of the various ports, and it said that greater efficiency could be brought about with the assistance of local committees. This would naturally create greater interest in boards of trade and the community in general, including longshoremen and workers on the waterfront. With a local committee representing these various groups, there would be general support. I do not say those committees must be given full authority, but, I feel that they should be in a position to advise; and certainly I believe they could advise more intelligently than men living a thousand miles away. In the east-and I believe it is the same in the west-this is referred to as a system of remote control.-This can be understood when it is realized that in Halifax we think of Ottawa being a thousand miles away. Quite often, from the attitude adopted by the minister and members of the national harbours board, I form the impression that, instead of their being a thousand miles away, they are ten thousand miles away, when they look at matters from Ottawa eastward.
To my mind there is a vast difference between trying to control a business from a thousand miles away and having someone right on the spot. We seldom see large concerns such as Eaton's and Simpson's following that practice-and I do not wish to advertise those companies. They set up local committees and give them full power to act. The}' do not just appoint a manager, as we appoint a port manager; they invest real authority in their local managers, so that they are permitted to do the buying and selling of merchandise and to carry on the business generally, under their own power.
On the contrary, this does not apply in respect of the ports. In Halifax an appointment cannot be made without the authority of the national harbours board. If a watchman is to be employed or given a permanent position, it must be approved by Ottawa. Perhaps in the first instance the recommendation would come from the local port manager, but the final approval must come from the board at Ottawa.
I am hopeful that, folio-wing the appointment today of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters) as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Transport, he will be able to do some of the things the minister
Suppl y-Transport

has not had time to do, and to come into closer contact with us on the east coast. He is a fine, bright, keen young man, and he appreciates our problems.
I venture to say that the national harbours board has not taken any direct or definite action to make sure that there is a sufficient quantity of grain in the elevators at Halifax at all times to meet the requirements of ships making regular calls at that port. Someone may say, "Oh, well, we have an elevator there of two million bushels capacity." That may be so, but it is never filled to capacity. We need that grain there at all times, to provide ballast for ships coming in and calling at our port.
I believe that if the figures are checked for the last ten years it will be found there has been a gradual decrease in the amount of grain shipped through Halifax-with the exception of one or two years when we waged a strong drive to have a few thousand bushels added for shipment to that port.
There are many local matters on wdiich the minister could be better advised by a local committee. I do not wish to speak at too great length, because I shall have an opportunity of asking questions later on; but I do hope that he will take definite action to provide local advisory committees composed of local men, with authority, so that they may advise intelligently those at Ottawa and thus bring to our port a greater amount of trade, and prevent trade which otherwise belongs to Canadian ports from being diverted to the United States.

Before the minister replies, I should like to say a word in support of my colleague who has been fighting the battle of the port of Halifax in this chamber since 1935. The minister has been asked to give further consideration to adopting a system of advisory committees to look after the interests of the various ports which come under the administration of the national harbours board. I would point out to the minister that the Gibb report recommended the setting up of a national harbours board to administer the Canadian harbours, but at the same time it pointed out the value of local advisory committees to assist the national board in properly looking after the interests of the various ports in this country, each of which has its own individual problems and interests which must be attended to.
I think it is unreasonable to expect that a national administration will be thoroughly satisfactory to all parts of the country, without there being local committees to assist and advise. For the last two years there has been at Halifax a port of Halifax club. This

is a private organization without any official standing, but its membership is made up of business and shipping men who have the interests of the port of Halifax at heart. If the minister will inquire from the port manager and the officials of the harbours board, I think he will find that that unofficial organization has made, in its short life, many constructive and helpful suggestions which have worked out to the mutual advantage of the club, the port of Halifax and the harbours board.
If an unofficial organization can make a contribution of that kind, I think it must be realized that a local advisory committee, having some official status and having definite duties, would be able to do much more. I hope the minister will give further serious consideration to the full implementation of the Gibb report. After all, the approval of the national harbours board in that report was to a large extent conditioned upon having local advisory committees to assist.

Mr. Chairman, coming from the other end of the country where there is a harbour of sorts, I want to say a word for fear the minister might too readily succumb to the eloquent pleadings of the senior and junior member for Halifax. The present system was adopted after another system had had many years of trial. I think the present system is much more satisfactory. The senior member for Halifax mentioned a committee with authority. If it is to be an advisory committee, it cannot be a committee with authority. If it is a committee with authority, it is something more than an advisory committee. In making any change in the present system the minister should be most careful.
I am all in favour of having advisory committees, but I know the dangers of small town machine politics in matters of this kind. If the minister needs any support in the matter and if mine is of any value, I shall be glad to give it to him.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. members for Halifax will expect me to say something. I say that, because the senior member at least has persistently brought this to my attention and to the attention of this house. Thus far the government has not seen fit to appoint local advisory committees, for the reasons which I have already given on other occasions and which perhaps I need not repeat in detail, but I do not say to the hon.

gentlemen that the question of advisory committees should not be given careful consideration.
In his report Sir Alexander Gibb recommended the appointment of local advisory committees, but on the other hand we must keep in mind that when reports are brought down they generally contain a number of recommendations which the government need not accept in their entirety. As far as the Gibb report is concerned, the government accepted some of the recommendations and did not deal with others. One of those which it did not act on was the appointment of local advisory committees. As such committees would have no financial responsibility, the government thought at the time that that recommendation should not be given effect to. I think now of the port of Toronto where a commission was set up under departmental jurisdiction and authority, but where the funds are provided, administered and spent by the city. The dominion government does not contribute to those expenditures.
The government felt that it would be much better if they were able to obtain outstanding men as port managers, men with experience, men who knew local conditions, men who were able to deal with local requirements, men who could meet with various groups in the community. We have been successful in getting two new port managers in recent years who, I think, are doing excellent work. The port manager at Halifax has had a great deal of experience. According to the information I have from my officers, he is able to meet and deal with various groups in the community.
My hon. friend says there is difficulty when one is far away from the central government, and to that I cannot take too much exception. There is bound to be criticism on that account. I have heard it in Vancouver; I have heard it in Halifax, and I have heard it also in Saint John. But one must keep in mind that when the National Harbours Board Act was passed and the board appointed, one of the objects was to avoid competition as between one port and another as there had been under the system which existed prior to 1937. If the government, through its national harbours board, were to encourage competition between the various ports, I do not know that that would tend to good administration. As it is now, the position of the port of Halifax so far as total cargo tonnage is concerned is good. In 1938 the total cargo tonnage was about 2.000,000 tons, and at the end of 1947 it was 3,577,000 tons, or an increase of more than one and a half million tons, which shows-
What was it in 1944?

speechtext: I will get that in a moment. That shows that the administration of the ports is progressing. I do not want to tell my hon. friend that I will not give consideration to the establishment of local advisory committees. The question comes up periodically, but thus far the government has not seen fit to establish them, for the reasons I have given. I am always open to conviction; as my hon. friend says, I now have the advantage of a new and young parliamentary assistant coming from the maritimes, and I am sure that he, too, will give this matter his very careful consideration.

I wish to thank the minister for his promise of consideration, although I never liked that word "consideration." I like "favourable review" very much better.
I should like to comment on the minister's remark that we do not want to set up competition between the various ports. That might sound all right to the minister, but if he considers the large commercial firms, wholesale and retail, which have branches throughout Canada, and the trust companies and the methods of banking institutions with branches spread all over the country from the east to the west, he will find that there is the keenest competition for business between the various branches. There are wholesale drug firms with branches in the province of New Brunswick, at Saint John, for instance, and Nova Scotia, at Halifax, all competing with one another for the business of the Annapolis valley and other sections of Nova Scotia. I do not think it was a particularly good argument which the minister advanced that competition is not a good thing, particularly as the policy of this government is, I believe, free enterprise. Incentive and competition are the life of business. I say to the minister that if you have the right type of man-and I believe you have in the majority of cases; you certainly have a very fine port manager at Halifax-if the opportunity were afforded to him of going out after business, the port of Halifax would get more business than it is now getting.

We have at least gained one point this evening by raising this question. I believe that there should be closer co-operation between these two bodies so far as Halifax is concerned. I promised the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario that I would make a statement on the policy of the government with reference to the expenditure of money on air services and air construction.
On April 2, 1943, a statement was made in this house by the Prime Minister relating to government policy with reference to civil aviation. Then on March 17, 1944, the Minister of Munitions and Supply reaffirmed that policy and extended it. Those statements give an accurate picture of government policy, although a few changes have been made and announced since that time. Additional changes will be made if and when new developments and conditions occur.
Enlarging somewhat on certain items of those previous statements, I should like to list the following responsibilities which the government has assumed:
1.	Commercial air services:
(a)	The establishment of trans-continental and main line services throughout Canada by Trans-Canada Air Lines, to a standard comparable with similar services in the United States, such services being based upon agreements between Trans-Canada Air Lines and the government, under the provisions of the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act.
(b>
The encouragement of feeder line schedule services throughout Canada, where present or future public convenience and necessity indicate that such services are required, such services to be provided to standard consistent with the traffic requirements.
(c)	The encouragement of frontier or "bush'' services, so -as to aid in the development of Canada's natural resources and adequately to provide for the development of those areas of Canada not served by other transportation facilities, where public interest indicates that such services are required.
(d)	The encouragement of the development of such specialty air services as are from time to time appropriate in the public interest.
(e)	The establishment of such international air services as are appropriate with Canada's interest in international trade routes.
2.	Airports:
(a)	The progressive development of main line airports, to permit of the utilization of the most modern types of aircraft at the minimum capital outlay consistent with safety and economy of operation.
(b)	The development of a minimum number of international airports consistent

. Supply-Transport
with Canada's position in the international civil aviation field and our obligations under international air agreements.
(c)	' The encouragement of and assistance to municipalities for the development of airports throughout Canada, where it seems desirable that such airports should be developed, maintained and operated by municipalities, to standards set out by the dominion government.
That deals more particularly with the first item that we discussed this evening.
(d)	The assistance in the establishment of airstrips at air bases feeding remote areas, for the purpose of stimulating the development of Canada's natural resources.
(e)	The assumption, for the time being, of part of the costs of maintenance and operation of those airports which are under the control of the Department of Transport, and to assist municipalities in the maintenance and operation of airports where such airports have either been transferred to, or developed by, municipalities.
In this connection, there has been established a scale of landing fees intended to meet part of the cost of the maintenance and operation of runways, which charges are based upon the ability of the air operator to pay and are approximately three per cent of the estimated revenue on a reasonable basis of operation.
Hangar rentals and other special facilities provided at airports at government expense are based upon a rental which is expected to amortize the cost involved over a reasonable period of time.
Efforts are being made to obtain revenues at the principal airports under the control of the Department of Transport, from such concessions as can be exploited with a view to meeting the expenses of maintenance and operation.
3.	Aids to air navigation:
The provision and maintenance of aerial aids to navigation, such as radio ranges, instrument landing systems, meteorological services and air traffic control, if necessary, so as to ensure the regularity and safety of air navigation.
4.	The government keeps abreast of all civil aviation developments. As a member of the international civil aviation organization, Canada has played a leading part in the establishment of common procedures in the technical aspects of civil aviation. The government will continue to favour the policy of international collaboration and co-operation in air transport.

I wish to say that I am not going to press this matter further at the moment; nevertheless I wish to make one or two comments to the minister about the statement which he read. What I asked the minister was for a statement showing the line of reasoning which had been used in air development, and particularly the relationship between the civil and the military side, the relation which defence had to ordinary commercial aviation. I think the minister will agree that the statement which he has read has said nothing about the security side, except by implication that these fields no doubt have a relation to security.
Any criticism that I make I realize is not levelled against the minister at all, because he has only just taken this branch over, and that is one of the reasons why I am not going to press the matter now. I think the statement he has given has in one way answered nothing. It has given us a certain number of figures. One could sum up by saying that it says we have felt it desirable to keep up with the Jones's; in other words, with other nations in the matter of civil aviation. I am not saying it is not a good thing. What I am saying is that it is no attempt to answer my question as to why we are carrying commercial passengers at a rate far below cost, which I assume we are. He has not answered that at all. He has not attempted to, but there is an important point in these expenditures which we are making for the defence element on the one side and the commercial element on the other. I will not press that now. I will

simply say that, so far as any evidence that we have at the present time indicates, there is no reason to suppose that there is any thought-out basis on which we are proceeding. We are simply going ahead in the belief that keping up aviation is a good thing-as I think it is-

speakeroldname: Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Before making
general observations, I was waiting for any other questions that hon. members might have wished to put. Perhaps I might start where the last speaker but one, the hon. member for Calgary West, left off, so that I can cover in a general way, at this stage, as many as possible of the points raised by those who have thus far discussed the estimates.
Of course it is difficult on these estimates, because of their particularity, to define the relationship between what is done under this vote and what might, within the rules of the house, more properly be discussed under the specific items to be contained in the supplementary estimates which will embrace the national health program announced a few
Supply-T ransport

weeks ago by the Prime Minister. But the question raised by the hon. member for Calgary West is one that I think comes under the general administrative vote; and perhaps on that account, and because of the importance of the matter, I should make a comment.
The hon. gentleman referred to what the department was doing with regard to one of the great causes of suffering in this country, namely rheumatism or, as it is more properly called, arthritis. A good part of what I would want to say about that subject, by the very nature of the program announced by the Prime Minister, would have to be discussed when we discuss our supplementary estimates in connection with the grants we intend to make to the provinces and which, among other things, in the public health grants, include some assistance toward trying to relieve human suffering in this country in terms of arthritis.
As the hon. gentleman has said, there is a general interest in this subject. Certain organizations throughout Canada have expressed a desire that provincial and federal administrations should seek to do something about this great cause of human suffering in our country. About nine months ago, having a layman's point of view in connection with this department, I asked two of my officials to go to England and to get in touch with Lord Horder, whose work in the field has perhaps been the most outstanding in the world. As a result of their conversations with him last September, I convoked here at Ottawa a conference of all the provincial governments, the medical colleges and the leading rheumatologists in this country, with the idea of seeing if there was something that we might do on a national basis to try to bring about co-ordinated action in regard to what is properly called arthritis.
The result of that meeting was the establishment in this country of an organization to be known as the Canadian arthritis and rheumatism society. The organization of the body followed the technique of the previously successful attempt in creating on a national basis the Canadian cancer institute. I am happy to say that the job of the Canadian arthritis society will be, first of all, to try to provide, through their films and pamphlets and whatever other known media are available, information which the specialists on this subject have-and I must say that I am advised it is a limited knowledge-with regard to the ways and means by which rheumatism, in the two hundred and over forms in which it exists, can best be corrected by medical action.
fMr. Martin.]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
By medical what?
Mr. MARTIN By medical and professional treatment. At the end of the last war the government in this country and the world generally, because they had in their midst tubercular veterans, were obliged by that fact to try to make some real effort to remove the scourge of tuberculosis. The impetus that was given by the Department of Veterans Affairs in this country, as well as by similar departments in other countries, sponsored by the obligation of 'looking after tubercular veterans, set on foot in this country a tremendous amount of governmental and voluntary effort in an attempt to remove tuberculosis from our midst. I have every reason to suggest that, as a result of world war II, it may be possible to duplicate in the arthritic field- and I am now merely expressing what I trust will ultimately prove to be an eventuality- the same kind of impetus that was given at the end of the last war. Why do I say that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Do your experts with respect to arthritis say that today they have any cure in the world for that disease?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No, I cannot say that they do. I shall come to that in a moment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That is all right. What I was trying to do was just to give the committee a picture of the imagination that has gone into what, in a humble way, we and the provinces are now attempting; and what we have done was done on the basis of the best professional advice existing in this country and in the United Kingdom. As a result of world war II, it may be expected that science, through the resources placed at its disposal by this nation for the treatment of arthritic veterans may bring about the same kind of encouragement that followed the action taken by the governments with regard to tubercular veterans at the end of the last war and its consequences on the civil population.
At Sunnybroolc hospital, which I understand many hon. members will visit tomorrow, and at one or two of our other major veterans hospitals in this country, but notably at Sunnybrook. there has been built in terms of

Supply-Trans purl
equipment, I am told-and I have never examined it; I am not personally qualified to comment on, to pass judgment on or to assess the value of that equipment, or to do other than rely upon what those who by training should know better about it-what is perhaps the most modern plant of its kind in the world. We are hoping that, as a result of that equipment, and as a result of the work of the rheumatism and arthritis society, as a result of the moneys which will be given by the central government to the provincial authorities, we may be able to do three things: first, to assist that society in carrying on an educational campaign in this country among those who are suffering from rheumatism, or arthritis as it is properly called; second, to give an impetus to the profession itself in the treatment of this subject. I hope it will be feasible to bring to Sunnybrook and to similar institutions in this country, for purposes of giving refresher courses with regard to arthritis, this terrible cause of suffering, certain people in the profession.
With regard to the specific question of the hon. member for Calgary West, whose great personal and national interest in this problem will, I am sure, commend itself to every member of the committee, because of his own close relation to it, we have had this conference with nine of the leading rheumatologists of this country, headed by Doctor Wallace Graham of Toronto, Doctor Wright of McGill and several others. We have relied on their judgment in the creation of this institute and society. The steps that we are taking to provide financial assistance to them, along with the moneys provided by the Canadian Red Cross will. I hope-and I cannot say any more at this stage than hope-set on foot a movement in this country which will at least partly relieve 100,000 people-that is an estimate based upon a survey made about seven years ago-who are seriously suffering from this disease, and perhaps another 700,000 who are not as seriously suffering.
I cannot at this time say any more than that about the matter. There is not as much known, so specialists say, as one would like. There are many forms of the disease which lend themselves to curative action, by rest treatment. But I wish to assure the hon. member and the committee that the interest I have taken personally with regard to the cancer institute-and I am not going to be overly modest about that achievement-will be as intense in this particular matter.
When we come to the supplementary estimates, once these matters are before the house I shall be able to indicate on the basis of
anticipated agreement with the provinces as a result of the conference of last Monday and Tuesday, what I might reasonably expect in terms of dollars and cents we might be able to do in trying to begin at long last to do something on a national basis in connection with this problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Research?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Research and treatment. Research in connection with arthritis is on a different basis. In the case of cancer, you can have research carried on in laboratories, as I shall ultimately indicate, as well as research carried on under treatment. In connection with arthritis, Doctor Wallace Graham, and these others tell me that there is a closer relationship between treatment and research. In other words, pure research in the case of arthritis does not exist as it does in cancer. You can more readily put a man to work in a laboratory on cancer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You have it right in front of you?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That is right. With regard to cancer, as I indicated last session to the house, it is one of the great killers, taking annually about 14,000 lives in this country. It seemed to us in the department that, while jurisdictionally health is a matter for the provinces, the same impetus which drove us to defeat the enemies of freedom should cause us to try to defeat the enemies of man in days of peace; and cancer is certainly one of those diseases and enemies.
I might say that in the Department of National Health and Welfare I have found this, that whatever may be the relationship between the provincial authorities and the central government, traditionally or actually, thanks to the successful functioning of the dominion council of health, I cannot, as Minister of National Health and Welfare, complain about the collaboration that I. as minister, have had with the provinces of Canada. Twice each year the dominion council of health meets to discuss in our department, under the chairmanship of the deputy minister of national health, problems of national and provincial interest in the field of health. Those conferences have allowed each of us to survey the field of national health without in any way creating the danger of intervening in places which are constitutionally reserved for other government authorities. And it was because of the experience at the first meeting of the dominion council of health which I attended a year ago. that last January we convoked a meeting of the cancer societies in Canada, the
Supply-T ransport

medical colleges in Canada, the provincial governments in Canada, the leading public bodies interested in providing financial assistance, the nursing association, and the like, with the thought of presenting to them this particular challenge, that, while in some provinces a special attempt was being made to eradicate or try to find some solution for cancer on the research side and to provide better diagnostic facilities and greater public information about the danger of cancer on the other, the time had come when we should try to co-ordinate in the national field what was now being done in several provincial jurisdictions. The result was the creation or the establishment of the National Cancer Institute of Canada.
I am pleased to say to the committee tonight that, as a result of that accomplishment, there began last September 12, twenty-seven different fundamental research projects on cancer in Canada. That, I think, is a significant achievement, for which I take no credit, and for which I am not asking that credit be given to the administration. The credit belongs to all who co-operated in creating that national body. That is in keeping with the tradition of this department, for our job on the national level is essentially and legally one of co-ordination of the activities carried on in the field of health by the various provinces.
When we come to the supplementary estimates I shall be able to indicate the financial assistance we are prepared to give, not only to the cancer institute but to the provinces, to enable them to carry on greater treatment facilities in respect of cancer, a greater system of education-and this is very important, because of the importance of early diagnosis- and greater financial resources to carry on research with regard to cancer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Diabetes, for example.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, diabetes is a good example. When Doctor Banting made his discovery it was based upon work done by a doctor at Yale, whose work in turn was being duplicated by scientists elsewhere.
I merely mention these two bodies to indicate that whatever may be the constitutional difficulties, there has grown up an opportunity through the dominion council of health to circumvent provincial boundaries to try to get common agreement with respect to action, and a proper assessment of which body is best fitted by any standard to deal with particular health problems. When, as I say, we come to the supplementary estimates I shall be able to particularize in much greater detail.
Then, the hon. member from Winnipeg spoke about treatment of the blind. Let me say simply this, that I cannot disagree with what he said, for I feel that this is a field where caution should not be underlined. What we all want, regardless of party, is to do the best we can in this important field of human endeavour.
I agree in the main with what he has said with regard to spending too much. There is something I should like to tell the committee, and I think this is the first time it has been said. Last year we reduced the age at which blind people could receive what I think is improperly called an old age pension-it is a pension which is paid under the Old Age Pensions Act-from forty to twenty-one years. I suggested to my officers that we should at once give consideration to the implications of the step we were taking and ask ourselves whether we were doing enough to prevent blindness, whether we were doing enough to try to improve the eyesight of people who, unless improvement was brought about, would ultimately grow into total blindness and be beyond the pale of improvement.
We have now proposed a scheme to all the provinces whereby, if they agree to spend twenty-five cents, we will contribute seventy-five cents toward the treatment of selected cases from among those people in receipt of pensions who are partially blind and try to improve their eyesight in the expectancy that such improvement will not only give them the freedom they want but will also relieve them from the pension rolls. Thus far we have

been able to conclude one agreement, with the province of New Brunswick, but I have every hope and expectancy that within the next few months we shall be able to conclude similar agreements with all the provinces. Thus a man of, say twenty-three years of age with thirty per cent vision, who is in receipt of a pension under the pensions act will be taken in hand to see what we can do to improve his eyesight and take him off the pension roll. This policy will be vigorously pursued.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is this proposal being made to the provinces apart from the program recently announced by the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It is a separate program. Mention has been made that we are spending more now in this department by some $80,000,000 than is being spent in the Department of National Defence. Roughly speaking, that is true. I am glad to say that is true. I do not for one moment minimize the importance of national defence at this time in our history, but I do think that if there is one department-I am assuming now that the money appropriated is properly spent-where we cannot measure results by dollars and cents, it is surely this department.
Without being adjudged irresponsible, I have endeavoured to put forward the point of view that wherever we can, by ourselves or in collaboration with the provinces, bring about improvement in health standards of our people, we should seek to do so. That is the only apology I have to offer for our expenditures. I am not referring to that as criticism by the hon. member for Eglinton, because he did not offer it in that vein. It was simply an observation he made, pointing out the growing importance of the department.

speechtext: That is the best kind of defence.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
As someone says, I think that is a pretty good kind of defence. The hon. member for Eglinton asked a number of questions. He asked about medical research. As the committee knows, there is provision in the new national health program for research on a basis higher than we have ever gone before and, I find on examination, higher than any other federal state in the world. When we come to those estimates I shall be glad to particularize.
In the meantime I can indicate that through the national research council, medical division,
the sum of $300,000 is currently being spent in the field of medical research. The Department of Veterans Affairs carries on clinical research in its major centres, notably, as I indicated earlier, with regard to arthritis. The Department of National Health and Welfare supports research projects in connection with the administration of Indian and Eskimo medical services.
I should' like to make a digression at this stage. With regard to tuberculosis, the fact is that one per cent of our population is responsible for twelve per cent of the tuberculosis we have in this country. The tubercular rate is very high among our Indians and Eskimos. It may be that some day someone may be open to criticism for the amount of money we are spending in this field, but I make no apology for it. In 1927 we were spending about $700,000 on Indian health; last year we spent $5,000,000, and this year we are going to spend approximately $7,500,000.
I am not saying that is adequate by any means, but it is adequate in relation to our ability to get the necessary professional skill to keep in touch with and be consistent with the program we are gradually developing. Hon. members who live in western Canada will appreciate the work being done by the Indian health section of this department. There is our Charles Camsell hospital at Edmonton with 350 beds. I am told by those who are in a better position to know that it is one of the best tubercular institutions in Canada.
There is our institution at Coqualeetza with 200 beds and the new hospital at Nanaimo which ultimately will have 200 beds. Then there is the hospital at Brandon with 200 beds and at The Pas with 185 beds. These are institutions devoted exclusively to the cure of tuberculosis among Indians and Eskimos and they represent a program which was begun nearly two years ago.
Hospital costs which are terrific are increasing the budget of this section of the department. This represents an attempt to deal with 130,000 people, the total of our Indian and Eskimo population. I am sure the committee, regardless of political affiliation, will join with me in saying that we owe an obligation to these people to try to remove this terrible scourge from their midst. In doing that, we help ourselves, because in those areas where the native population is contiguous to the white population, one frequently finds that the tubercular rate among the white population is higher than in other centres further removed from the native population. So quite apart from the question of duty there is the question of self-interest. I do not want to

But he did raise one matter that I should like to mention to the committee now, so that the members will have these figures before them when they are considering the supplementary estimates in relation to the new health program of the government.
I have reference to hospital admissions in Canada. The reports of the dominion bureau of statistics show that the number of hospital admissions in Canaria increased from 574.489 in 1938 to 1,365,928 in 1945. To put it in another way, the index has risen from a base of 100 to 237. Comparable figures on the number of beds are not immediately available. However, the total number of patient-under hospital care rose from 58 per 1.000 of population in 1932 to 110 per 1,000 in 1944. Many factors enter into this. There is a greater tendency to use hospitals, on account of changes in the way we live and changes in medical practice. There is also a more rapid turnover of patients, as a result of the shortening of many illnesses by the use of new drugs such as penicillin, which means that one bed serves more patients than ever before, and there is also the spread of health insurance schemes, all of which have played a part in changing the statistical picture.
The hon. member for Eglinton asked a question with regard to T.B. statistics. The figures for 1947 are not yet available. The increase mentioned by the hon. gentleman between
1945	and 1946 is probably not significant when the general trend is noted. The death rate in 1900 was 200 per 100.000 of population, and in

The last observation I want to make in a general way at this stage is that the estimates this year are naturally over-shadowed by the important announcement made by the Prime Minister, but I wish to say at this stage that we did have on Monday and Tuesday of this week-I am not now going to give the results of our conference with the provinces-an exploratory conference with them which I think I can describe as being more than satisfactory. There is a great deal of ground work to be done. The provinces have to appraise their situation, and giving them this opportunity to assess their needs and exchange information with us may well mean the saving of some weeks. Is it on the increase as compared with the increase of population in the country? I think the minister understands what I have in mind. I realize fully that in these days more people are using the hospitals than they did formerly. For instance, many years ago babies were born at home and mothers were not hospitalized. That day has gone, and was gone prior to the year the minister gave me. I know that many mothers go to the hospital; my own wife, for example. I have a child thirty-five years of age. She is not exactly a child, but she was once. My children were born at home. I was opposed to the idea but naturally I did not count in that picture.
Take mining camps. This is where the doctors are bright. In a mining camp you usually have a hospital which is owned by the miners themselves. This is the way it operates in the part of the country from which I come. I do not see many doctors in the house at the moment. There are two here. Instead of going to the miner's home, the doctors found that it was much simpler to send him to the hospital. They had a contract with the hospital, and they can take care of half a dozen men in the hospital at one time instead of calling at half a dozen homes. I am not saying this in criticism. Were I a doctor I would do the same thing and perhaps do a great deal more of it and thereby save time for other people.
I pass along to one remark the minister made which I should like him to clarify. He said that the white population, contiguous to Indian reservations or to Eskimo people, were more subject to tuberculosis than other whites in Canada. I should like to ask whether or not the minister thinks active operation of tuberculosis among Indians and Eskimos can possibly have anything to do with that? In other words, is not the cause of tuberculosis among these people largely the conditions under which the patient, as he becomes later, is living? Does the minister really think the white population are infected with tuberculosis because they are living alongside Indians?

I now turn to what I began with, namely arthritis. Do I summarize the position correctly when I say this? May I say, Mr. Chairman, that I say this without even a thought of blaming t'he minister, the department or anyone else. Is this not the present position with respect to arthritis? No one in the world today knows the cause of it. I think that is a fair statement. In January I myself spent a couple of weeks at perhaps the most famous institution of its kind in the world, and I certainly got that impression from the place in which I was. The minister said he hoped that, following this war, we would get the impetus that the investigation of tuberculosis received after the first great war. All of us will, I am sure, join the minister in that hope. But does it not resolve itself to this? By research, and particularly by treatment, because treatment is research-I mean a doctor has a dozen cases-a doctor learns something. An institution has a dozen cases. The doctor is in a much better position to make comparisons and therefore come to a conclusion which is more likely to be right than the conclusion of a person who has only a few cases.
I want to say just a word about an institution at Banff.

In this House of Commons we must not mention names or do anything of that kind. But is it not more likely that, by segregating these people in a place where many observations can be made by competent medical people, we shall more quickly arrive at a conclusion as to the origin of the disease and its treatment? Today, as I understand it, all we can do is to ease the pain. At the moment we know nothing as to the origin of the disease or as to its eradication. The only thing we can do at the moment is to ease the suffering of these people.

The minister gave some figures which are even higher than I thought they were. We in Canada have a population of around twelve million people. The minister mentioned that a hundred thousand people were suffering severely. From -that, I gather that the people to whom he referred were crippled by this disease. He then said that possibly 700,000-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Between 700,000 and 800,000. That is based upon a survey of 1938.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
What does that mean? We are a population of twelve million people. Of that number 800,000 or
900.000	are suffering the pains of arthritis. I speak with some knowledge. I have just a little idea of what they are going through. I am one of those fortunate people in whom the disease was arrested. My good friend, the hon. member for Lanark, told me that sometimes the disease did arrest itself. I happened to be one of the hundreds to whom that happened. When it will start again I have no idea. But when we admit that 800,000 or
900.000	people out of 12,000,000-and it affects people of all ages-one-thirteenth or one-fourteenth of our total population are suffering and are apt to be crippled by this illness, then it seems to me that we have never known a greater national emergency.
Let us put it in this way. For the moment leave out the faculty of human suffering. Let us accept it on the basis of our economy. You take 800,000 out of 12,000,000 and you have cut down your working force, your earning force, your producing force. You have taken that number from our economy, because the minister will admit that the incidence below manhood and womanhood is not large. It does strike down young people, it is true, but I do not think the incidence among children is nearly so heavy as it is among those who have gone on to manhood and womanhood.
I give the minister credit; I honour him, for the conferences which he has called. I say to the members of this committee that no war has ever removed from our working forces that number of people, and one hesitates to contemplate the mass suffering which goes on among 800,000 people. If that is not a national emergency I never knew one.
As far as I am concerned, and I am sure I speak for all members of the committee, I will uphold the minister's hands in every way I can. Let us regard it from the economic side, if you like, a matter of money. But let us not do that. Let us rather be humanitarian and save these poor people from suffering, which is unnecessary if we can only find the remedy. Why have we not found it?

I have consulted many physicians, and they have given me the same answer. I say, "Why is it that there are so many people suffering from rheumatism?" I am told by competent X-ray people that I have enough rheumatism in my back to cripple me, but still I can dance a jig the odd time if I have sufficient fortification from the hon. member for Davenport. However, they all tell me that the reason we have not advanced further is that, while it is chronic, it is not fatal. That is true, and it is a statement which reflects no credit on the people of Canada or on the House of Commons.
Once more I assure, indeed I reassure, the minister that I will support him to the limit, as I am sure the house will, in any measures he can reasonably take to eliminate this scourge of all scourges, speaking of pain, from our midst.

The result was that he backed up a former promise that a grant would be made by the dominion government to build an extension to our sanatorium. The report I received yesterday was that this extension has been made possible by this grant. On behalf of the board, I express our appreciation to the minister and his workers.
One other thing. During the past year, or more nearly two years, a new treatment has been introduced for tuberculosis. It is known as streptomycin. It is injected, and I can assure the committee that it works. But it costs a great deal. When it first came out it cost 83,000. and then it was cut down to nearly half. I have a close friend who took the treatment. At Christmas he collapsed, and now he is being discharged from the hospital by the first of July as cured. I hope this treatment can be made available to people who cannot pay 81,400 or more. Once more I express, on behalf of the sanatorium board, appreciation of the work of the minister and the splendid results that have followed.

I had not expected to speak on this subject again because, as I stated before
the dinner recess, I wished to reserve my talk on matters of health until the introduction of the supplementary estimates, but the hon. member for Calgary West has introduced the question of arthritis. I have never missed a chance to say something about arthritis. It seems to be a hopeless disease and in the past it has been regarded in that light. When I say it is hopeless, I mean we have not yet found a cure for it. Research has been carried on, but we have not found a cure.
A situation has arisen where, in the public hospitals, in the small hospitals in the towns, and the city hospitals, the main public wards are filled with these people. Many of them have spent valuable resources in trying to get better. They get into the public wards and there they fill beds which are required for acute cases.
The hon. member mentioned 600,000 cases of chronic arthritis, but there are 125,000 acutely suffering. The point I make, however, is this. I was interested in the minister's account of what is being done at Sunnybrook. I have criticized that program before and I intend to criticize it again, because I do not feel that it is reaching the general medical practitioner. It is not reaching the man who has to do with cases. It is not reaching the medical schools, and nothing is being done in that way. While Sunnybrook can do research, and we are glad it is helping returned soldiers, it is not reaching the mass of the population.
It is all very well to carry on there, but I have seen patients in the public wards because there was nowhere else for them to go. The main thing is that if we are to deal with this problem we must start at the root of things.
Mention is made of specialists in arthritis. I do not know where they are, because you cannot specialize in something when you do not know the answer. I will say, however, that there are pseudospecialists who are taking advantage of these people by offering certain cures and taking their money, while little result is shown. We can, however, do something with this disease in the way of stopping some of these people from becoming hopeless cripples, and that requires, as has been suggested, some special apparatus. Some of this material is not available to general practitioners who come into contact with the greater number of patients.
Physiotherapy can do a great deal, and bed rest, complete rest. The hon. member for Calgary West mentioned hospitalization, and so did the minister later. This also comes into the question of arthritis. People are going into the hospital now for the reason that there is a

shortage of trained nurses in Canada. You cannot get a trained nurse any place. The other thing is the shortage of help in the home. Industrial plants have bought industrial health insurance for their people. People are afraid of the high cost of sickness. They just cannot afford to be sick.	.
But to get back to the people who are suffering from arthritis, in spite of the fact that I do not pose as a specialist, I have had practical experience in seeing these poor people who suffer. I cannot feel that a start in coping with this disease has been accomplished at Sunnybrook. You are only dealing with a specialized bunch of people.
